docs.title: Welcome
docs.text: Run Envoy Gateway on AWS managed Envoy proxies with Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) for Envoy

docs.title: ELB Envoy Remote Infra Provider
docs.text:
elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider is an open source controller that runs the Envoy data plane for Envoy Gateway on ELB for Envoy, instead of on Envoy pods in your cluster. ELB for Envoy runs, scales, and patches the Envoy proxies for you.

Envoy Gateway works the same way it does with in-cluster Envoy: it watches your Gateway API resources and computes Envoy configuration. The controller creates one ELB for Envoy proxy for each Gateway, and that proxy runs the configuration. You keep the Gateway API workflow.

The following diagram shows the flow from your Gateway API resources to a running proxy.

  1. You apply Gateway API resources and an ELBProxyConfiguration.
  2. Envoy Gateway translates them into Envoy configuration.
  3. Envoy Gateway sends the Gateway's infrastructure to the sidecar over a Unix socket.
  4. The sidecar provisions a managed Envoy proxy through the ELB for Envoy API.
  5. The proxy gets its routes and clusters from Envoy Gateway over xDS.
  6. Clients connect to the Gateway address, and the proxy sends traffic to your pods.

For the full picture, see How it works.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Creates one ELB for Envoy proxy for each Gateway. Attach an ELBProxyConfiguration to a Gateway or GatewayClass, and the controller creates and manages the proxy. With merged gateways, it creates one proxy for each GatewayClass.
  • Keeps Envoy Gateway as the control plane. The proxy gets its routes and clusters from Envoy Gateway over xDS, so HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, TCPRoute, TLSRoute, and UDPRoute are all supported. A few Envoy Gateway features differ. See Compatibility.
  • Manages networking. By default, it discovers subnets, creates security groups for the proxy, and opens the node security group rules the proxy needs to reach your pods.
  • Publishes the Gateway address. The proxy's DNS name becomes the Gateway's address.
  • Cleans up. Deleting a Gateway deletes its proxy and the security groups the controller created.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
1. Install the controller and Envoy Gateway.
  2. Deploy your first Gateway on an AWS managed proxy.
  3. Tune the proxy with ELBProxyConfiguration and the controller flags.

Check Compatibility for supported versions, and Troubleshooting if you encounter issues.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster on Amazon EC2, such as Amazon EKS, with a Kubernetes version supported by your Envoy Gateway release
  • Gateway API v1.6 or later standard channel CRDs, including ListenerSet
  • Envoy Gateway, configured as a remote infrastructure provider, with its leader election disabled
  • Pod IPs routable in the virtual private cloud (VPC), for example with the Amazon VPC CNI

See Compatibility for details.

docs.title: Version matrix
docs.text:
The following table lists the versions this controller release supports.

Controller Envoy Gateway Envoy Proxy Gateway API Kubernetes v1.0.0 v1.10 1.40 v1.6.1 v1.34, v1.35, v1.36, v1.37
  • Envoy Gateway: the version this controller release is built and tested against. Envoy Gateway must be configured as a remote infrastructure provider (infrastructure.type: Remote).
  • Envoy Proxy: the Envoy minor version that the Envoy Gateway release in that row generates configuration for. The controller creates every proxy with this version, taken from the Envoy Gateway version it's built against, not the one running in your cluster. You can't choose a different version, and the controller doesn't change the version of an existing proxy.
  • Gateway API and Kubernetes: follow the Envoy Gateway release. The controller also requires Kubernetes 1.29 or later for native sidecars, which every version in this range meets.

The Envoy Proxy, Gateway API, and Kubernetes versions for each Envoy Gateway release come from the Envoy Gateway compatibility matrix.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Upgrade Envoy Gateway and the controller together, to the versions in the same row of the version matrix. Each Envoy Gateway release generates configuration for a single Envoy minor version, and the controller creates proxies with the Envoy version of the Envoy Gateway release it's built against. A newer Envoy Gateway than the matrix lists can generate configuration for an Envoy version that your proxies don't run. This combination isn't supported.

Upgrading the controller doesn't change the Envoy version of existing proxies. A proxy keeps the version it was created with.

docs.title: Envoy Gateway features
docs.text:
The proxy runs the configuration Envoy Gateway generates, so Gateway API and Envoy Gateway features work as described in the Envoy Gateway documentation, for the Envoy Gateway version in the matrix above.

Because the proxy runs in AWS instead of in your cluster, a few things differ. The following table lists them.

Feature Difference EnvoyProxy settings The controller doesn't pass provider.kubernetes (replicas, autoscaling, disruption budgets, Service type and annotations, pod patches), concurrency, extraArgs, or shutdown to the proxy, because AWS runs and scales it. Other EnvoyProxy settings, such as routingType and filterOrder, change the xDS configuration that Envoy Gateway generates, so they still apply. Access logs Must be disabled or use an OpenTelemetry or Access Log Service (ALS) sink. The controller rejects file sinks, including the default /dev/stdout. See Observability. Global rate limiting Not supported. Envoy Gateway doesn't deploy its rate limit service with a remote infrastructure provider, and it points proxies at that service's cluster DNS name, which doesn't resolve outside the cluster. A BackendTrafficPolicy with type: Global either isn't enforced or fails every request on its routes. Which one happens depends on failClosed. Use local rate limiting instead. See Global rate limiting doesn't work. Local rate limiting Supported. type: Local needs no extra service. Each proxy instance counts separately, so the effective limit is the configured limit times the number of instances serving traffic. Merged gateways One AWS proxy per GatewayClass. Standalone (non-Kubernetes) Envoy Gateway Not supported.

docs.title: Platform requirements
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are Amazon EC2 instances in the same virtual private cloud (VPC) as the proxy, such as an Amazon EKS cluster. The controller finds each node's EC2 instance from the node's spec.providerID, so the nodes need an AWS provider ID, which the AWS cloud provider sets. On a cluster that isn't Amazon EKS, also tag the node security groups kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name>, with the value owned or shared.
  • Gateway API CRDs from the standard channel, v1.6 or later, including TCPRoute, TLSRoute, UDPRoute, and ListenerSet at gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1. The controller watches all of them and doesn't skip one whose CRD is missing, so install them all, even if you don't use every kind.
  • AWS credentials for the Envoy Gateway pod, from any source that the default credential chain of the AWS SDK supports. The Installation Guide shows EKS Pod Identity and IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA).
  • Pod IPs routable in the VPC, for example with the Amazon VPC CNI. The proxy connects directly to Envoy Gateway and backend pod IPs. Overlay networks, such as Calico with VXLAN or flannel, don't meet this requirement. If your pods have their own security groups, add the security group rules for them yourself. See Node security group rules.
  • Envoy Gateway's leader election disabled. See How it works.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Envoy Gateway normally runs Envoy as a Deployment inside your cluster. With elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider, Envoy Gateway still does all the Gateway API work, but Envoy itself runs on an AWS managed proxy from Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) for Envoy. The controller is the bridge: it takes the infrastructure Envoy Gateway asks for and creates the matching AWS proxy.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The following diagram shows how the components connect.

flowchart LR
  subgraph cluster["Kubernetes cluster"]
    subgraph egpod["Envoy Gateway pod"]
      eg["envoy-gateway"]
      sc["elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider<br/>(native sidecar)"]
      eg -- "gRPC over Unix socket<br/>(infrastructure IR)" --> sc
    end
    pods["Backend pods"]
  end
  subgraph aws["AWS"]
    proxy["ELB for Envoy"]
  end
  sc -- "ELB for Envoy and EC2 APIs" --> proxy
  proxy -- "xDS (mTLS, port 18000)" --> eg
  proxy -- "traffic" --> pods
  client["Clients"] --> proxy

The following table describes each component.

Component Where it runs What it does Envoy Gateway Envoy Gateway pod Watches Gateway API resources, computes Envoy config, and serves it over xDS. Configured with a remote infrastructure provider, so it doesn't create Envoy Deployments itself. ELB Envoy Remote Infra Provider Envoy Gateway pod, as a native sidecar Receives infrastructure requests from Envoy Gateway and creates, updates, and deletes AWS proxies and security groups. ELB for Envoy AWS Runs Envoy. Gets its routes and clusters from Envoy Gateway over xDS, and sends traffic to your pods.

docs.title: From Gateway to ELB proxy
docs.text:
1. You create a Gateway. Envoy Gateway processes it as usual and builds the infrastructure for it: listeners, ports, and the EnvoyProxy settings.
  2. Envoy Gateway calls the sidecar. Instead of creating a Deployment, Envoy Gateway sends this infrastructure to the sidecar over gRPC on a Unix socket shared in the pod. The sidecar caches it and returns immediately, so Envoy Gateway never waits on AWS.
  3. The controller finds the ELBProxyConfiguration. Each Gateway needs an ELBProxyConfiguration attached to it. Without one, the controller creates nothing on AWS.
  4. The controller creates AWS resources. It builds a model of the resources the Gateway needs and deploys it in order:
    1. Security groups
    2. The proxy, with its network settings, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, tags, and Envoy configuration
    3. A Kubernetes Service that carries the proxy's address
  5. The Gateway gets an address. When the proxy is ready, the controller writes the proxy's DNS name into that Service's load balancer status. Envoy Gateway picks it up and publishes it as the Gateway's address.

Provisioning a new proxy takes several minutes. While the proxy is being created, the controller checks again every 2 minutes. To follow progress, see Status and events.

docs.title: How the proxy gets its configuration
docs.text:
The controller pushes two things to each proxy through the ELB for Envoy API:

  • Bootstrap: the Envoy bootstrap, built the same way Envoy Gateway builds it for in-cluster Envoy, including any EnvoyProxy.spec.bootstrap customization. It points Envoy at Envoy Gateway's xDS server and identifies which Gateway this proxy serves.
  • Config archive: three things Envoy needs: the TLS client certificate, private key, and CA it uses to connect to Envoy Gateway; the Envoy Gateway pod IPs to connect to, for xDS and for Wasm modules; and the Availability Zones of the proxy's subnets (local_cluster), which zone-aware routing needs. Every proxy in the cluster gets the same certificate and key, copied from Envoy Gateway's certs.

After that, the proxy gets routes, clusters, and endpoints live from Envoy Gateway over xDS. It connects directly to the Envoy Gateway pod IPs on port 18000 using mutual TLS (mTLS). For Wasm extensions, it downloads modules from Envoy Gateway's Wasm server on port 18002.

The controller compares hashes and only pushes the parts that changed. A new push happens when:

  • Envoy Gateway sends new infrastructure for the Gateway.
  • Envoy Gateway's TLS certificates rotate. The sidecar watches the cert files.
  • Envoy Gateway pod IPs change.
  • The ELBProxyConfiguration or a route changes.

docs.title: How traffic reaches your pods
docs.text:
The proxy sends traffic directly to pod IPs, using the endpoints Envoy Gateway serves over xDS. This requires pod IPs that are routable in the virtual private cloud (VPC), as with the Amazon VPC CNI.

To allow this traffic, the controller manages the security groups in the following table.

Security group Scope Rules Frontend SG One per Gateway Allows inbound traffic on each listener port from spec.ingressCidrs (default 0.0.0.0/0, plus ::/0 with IPv6) and spec.ingressPrefixLists. Shared backend SG One per controller install (cluster name and controller namespace), attached to every proxy that install manages Used as the source for the node security group rules below. Each install creates and revokes only its own backend SG and node SG rules, so installs in different namespaces don't interfere. Node SG rules Your existing node security groups Allows inbound traffic from the shared backend SG on TCP port 18000 (xDS) and TCP port 18002 (Wasm modules), both to Envoy Gateway, and on the target port of every Service the proxy sends traffic to: route backends, request mirror targets, and the ext_authz and ext_proc services of your SecurityPolicy and EnvoyExtensionPolicy resources. The two Envoy Gateway ports open as soon as a Gateway exists, before any route does.

Note

If you bring your own security groups with spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups, the controller uses them as they are. It doesn't create a frontend SG, doesn't add node SG rules, and ignores ingressCidrs and ingressPrefixLists. You must allow the traffic yourself: from the proxy to Envoy Gateway on port 18000 (xDS), and on port 18002 if you use Wasm extensions, and to your backend pods, request mirror targets, and ext_authz and ext_proc services on their target ports. See Security groups.

docs.title: High availability and leader election
docs.text:
Every Envoy Gateway replica has its own sidecar. All sidecars accept infrastructure from their Envoy Gateway container, but only one, the leader, calls AWS. The sidecars elect a leader with the lease elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-leader.

This is why Envoy Gateway's own leader election must be disabled. With it on, only the Envoy Gateway leader sends infrastructure, so the other sidecars' caches stay empty or stale. If leadership then moves to one of those sidecars, it would act on stale data. With it off, every replica keeps its sidecar up to date, and the sidecar lease picks the single writer.

Disable it in the Envoy Gateway configuration:

provider:
  type: Custom
  custom:
    resource:
      type: Kubernetes
      kubernetes:
        leaderElection:
          disable: true
    infrastructure:
      type: Remote
      remote:
        service:
          unix:
            path: /var/run/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider/server.sock

See Installation Guide Step 4 for the full setup. For how Envoy Gateway's leader election and remote infrastructure provider work, see the Envoy Gateway documentation.

docs.title: Merged gateways
docs.text: If you enable Envoy Gateway's merged gateways mode, Envoy Gateway sends one set of infrastructure for the whole GatewayClass. The controller then creates one proxy for all Gateways in the class. In this mode, only an ELBProxyConfiguration that targets the GatewayClass applies.

docs.title: Deletion and cleanup
docs.text:
When you delete a Gateway:

  1. Envoy Gateway tells the sidecar to delete the infrastructure.
  2. The controller removes node SG rules for ports no other Gateway needs. The two Envoy Gateway ports stay open while any Gateway exists.
  3. The controller deletes the Service.
  4. The controller deletes the proxy and waits until it's gone. It checks every 30 seconds.
  5. Then it deletes the frontend SG. The shared backend SG is removed when no Gateway uses it.

An ELBProxyConfiguration has a finalizer. You can't delete it while a Gateway still uses it.

docs.title: Drift and recovery
docs.text:
• Every reconcile corrects drift. The controller compares the live proxy's configuration, attributes, network settings, and tags with the desired state and fixes differences.
  • Some settings replace the proxy. name, roleArn, and the IP configuration can't change on an existing proxy. Changing one deletes the old proxy and creates a new one, and the Gateway gets a new address.
  • Restarts. When a new leader starts and has no infrastructure yet, it finds existing proxies by their tags, so it can keep managing them.
  • Garbage collection. Every 60 minutes, it looks for proxies whose Gateway is gone, and for orphaned security groups.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
The controller tags everything it creates so it can find its own resources and so the IAM policy can scope write access. The following table lists the tag keys.

Tag key Meaning gateway.elbproxy.aws/cluster Cluster name gateway.elbproxy.aws/stack The Gateway (namespace/name) or merged GatewayClass that owns the resource gateway.elbproxy.aws/resource Resource type gateway.elbproxy.aws/managed-by Marks the resource as managed by this controller gateway.elbproxy.aws/controller-ns Namespace of the controller install that owns the shared backend SG gateway.elbproxy.aws/deploy-mode Marks resources created for a merged GatewayClass

You can add your own tags with spec.tags on the ELBProxyConfiguration or the controller's --default-tags flag. When both set the same key, spec.tags wins. Keys listed in --external-managed-tags are left to other systems on proxies: the controller never adds, changes, or removes them there, and setting one in spec.tags is an error. This doesn't apply to security groups. The controller removes any tag it didn't set from the security groups it creates. Don't use keys that start with gateway.elbproxy.aws/. See Configurations.

docs.title: Controller configuration options
docs.text:
This page covers the command-line flags of the elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider binary.

The binary runs in two places:

  • Sidecar: runs inside the Envoy Gateway pod. It serves the gRPC socket Envoy Gateway calls and manages the AWS resources.
  • Webhook deployment (optional): installed by the Helm chart when webhook.enabled=true. It runs the mutating webhook that injects the sidecar into the Envoy Gateway pod.

Most of these flags configure the sidecar. Where you set them depends on how you add the sidecar. See Installation Guide.

docs.title: Setting sidecar flags
docs.text:
Envoy Gateway Helm values (default)Webhook

Set flags directly in the sidecar's args in your Envoy Gateway values (based on k8s/envoy-gateway-values.yaml):

deployment:
  pod:
    initContainers:
      - name: elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider
        args:
          - --server-socket-path=/var/run/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider/server.sock
          - --cluster-name=my-cluster
          - --aws-region=us-west-2
          - --aws-vpc-id=vpc-0123456789abcdef0
          - --default-tags=team=platform,env=prod

The chart turns clusterName, aws.region, and aws.vpcId into sidecar flags. Add any other sidecar flag to webhook.sidecar.extraArgs, one flag per entry:

clusterName: my-cluster         # --cluster-name (required)
aws:
  region: us-west-2             # --aws-region
  vpcId: vpc-0123456789abcdef0  # --aws-vpc-id
webhook:
  enabled: true
  sidecar:
    extraArgs:
      - --default-tags=team=platform,env=prod
      - --aws-api-endpoints=EC2=https://ec2.example.com

The webhook passes each entry to the sidecar unchanged, so values that contain commas work. Don't repeat clusterName, aws.region, or aws.vpcId there.

The chart's top-level extraArgs and env apply to the webhook deployment only. They don't reach the sidecar.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
The following table lists the general flags.

Flag Type Default Description cluster-name string CLUSTER_NAME environment variable Kubernetes cluster name. Used to tag the AWS resources the controller creates. log-level string info Log level: debug, info, or error. metrics-bind-address string :8082 Address the metrics server binds to. Defaults to :8082 to avoid Envoy Gateway's :8080. leader-election-namespace string POD_NAMESPACE environment variable Namespace for the leader election lease. sync-period duration 10h0m0s Period at which the controller forces a resync of its local object stores. server-socket-path string /var/run/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider/server.sock Path of the gRPC Unix domain socket the server listens on. server-socket-mode uint32 0660 File mode (octal) applied to the socket file.

docs.title: AWS
docs.text:
The following table lists the flags that configure AWS access.

Flag Type Default Description aws-region string AWS_REGION / AWS_DEFAULT_REGION environment variable AWS Region of the cluster. The controller fails to start if no region is resolved. aws-vpc-id string auto-detected VPC for the proxy resources. See VPC detection. aws-vpc-tags stringMap Find the VPC by tags instead of ID, for example env=prod,team=platform. Exactly one VPC must match. aws-max-attempts int 10 Total attempts (initial request plus retries) for AWS API calls. 0 uses the SDK default of 3. aws-api-endpoints stringMap Custom endpoint overrides, format serviceID1=URL1,serviceID2=URL2. Supported service IDs: EC2 and ELB Proxy. Useful for VPC endpoints or local testing.

docs.title: Tagging
docs.text:
The following table lists the flags that control AWS tags.

Flag Type Default Description default-tags stringMap AWS tags applied to every proxy, format key1=value1,key2=value2. Tags set on ELBProxyConfiguration take precedence. external-managed-tags stringList AWS tag keys on proxies that are managed outside the controller. The controller never adds, updates, or removes these keys on proxies. This doesn't apply to security groups: the controller removes any tag it didn't set from the security groups it creates.

The controller reserves these tag keys. They can't be used in default-tags or external-managed-tags:

  • gateway.elbproxy.aws/cluster
  • gateway.elbproxy.aws/stack
  • gateway.elbproxy.aws/resource
  • gateway.elbproxy.aws/managed-by

A key also can't appear in both default-tags and external-managed-tags.

Don't use any key that starts with gateway.elbproxy.aws/ in spec.tags or --default-tags. The controller rejects the four keys above only in the two flags, not in spec.tags, and it doesn't block the other keys with this prefix. A tag you set replaces the tag the controller uses to find its resources.

docs.title: Sidecar webhook
docs.text:
These flags apply only to the webhook deployment. The Helm chart sets them when webhook.enabled=true.

Flag Type Default Description enable-sidecar-webhook boolean false Run only the mutating webhook that injects the sidecar into the Envoy Gateway pod. webhook-bind-port int 9443 Port the webhook server listens on. webhook-cert-dir string /tmp/k8s-webhook-server/serving-certs Directory holding the webhook's tls.crt and tls.key. health-probe-bind-addr string :61779 Address the webhook serves /readyz on. Ready once the webhook server completes a TLS handshake. sidecar-image string Image injected as the sidecar. Required when enable-sidecar-webhook is set. sidecar-image-pull-policy string IfNotPresent Pull policy for the sidecar image: Always, IfNotPresent, or Never. sidecar-mount-certs boolean true Mount the Envoy Gateway certificates volume into the sidecar. sidecar-extra-args stringArray One flag to pass to the injected sidecar. Repeat for each flag. The chart sets this from clusterName, aws.region, aws.vpcId, and webhook.sidecar.extraArgs.

docs.title: VPC detection
docs.text:
When aws-vpc-id isn't set, the controller resolves the virtual private cloud (VPC) in this order:

  1. If aws-vpc-tags is set, it looks up the single VPC matching all the tags.
  2. Otherwise, it reads an EC2 instance ID from the NODENAME environment variable and looks up that instance's VPC.

Tip

Set aws-vpc-id explicitly. Neither install option sets NODENAME, so the second step fails unless you set it yourself. If the controller can't resolve the VPC, it fails to start with the error NODENAME "" is not an instance ID.

docs.title: What the injected sidecar receives
docs.text:
With the webhook, the injected sidecar gets:

  • --server-socket-path, set by the webhook to match the shared socket volume.
  • Every --sidecar-extra-args value, as its own flag, in order. This includes the flags the chart builds from clusterName, aws.region, and aws.vpcId.
  • The ENVOY_GATEWAY_NAMESPACE and POD_NAMESPACE environment variables.

The webhook doesn't forward any of its own other flags. When aws.region is empty, the sidecar falls back to the AWS_REGION environment variable, which IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) set. Set aws.region to avoid depending on it.

Warning

Don't override --server-socket-path in webhook.sidecar.extraArgs. It must match Envoy Gateway's socket path and the sidecar's mounts and probes.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text:
elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider connects Envoy Gateway to ELB for Envoy (AWS managed Envoy). It runs as a sidecar inside the Envoy Gateway pod. Envoy Gateway sends it the infrastructure for each Gateway, and the sidecar creates and manages the matching AWS proxy.

The Helm chart installs:

  • The ELBProxyConfiguration CRD.
  • RBAC for the sidecar, bound to the Envoy Gateway service account.
  • Optionally, a mutating webhook that injects the sidecar into the Envoy Gateway pod.

The chart does not install Envoy Gateway. You install and configure it yourself in Step 4.

Tip

If you already run Envoy Gateway with in-cluster Envoy, don't switch your existing install to remote. Follow Migrating from in-cluster Envoy instead.

docs.title: Choose how to add the sidecar
docs.text:
The controller runs as an extra container (a sidecar) in the Envoy Gateway pod. You can add that container in one of two ways:

  • Envoy Gateway Helm values (default). You put the sidecar definition in the Helm values that you use to install Envoy Gateway. No other component runs in your cluster. The file k8s/envoy-gateway-values.yaml contains the definition.
  • Webhook. You install a webhook from this chart. When Envoy Gateway's pod is created, the webhook adds the sidecar. Choose this only if you can't change Envoy Gateway's Helm values. The webhook needs its own deployment and TLS certificate. With the default failurePolicy: Fail, Envoy Gateway pods can't be created while the webhook is down.

The sidecar behaves the same in both options. Steps 3 and 4 have a tab for each option. Use the same option in both steps.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster running a version supported by Envoy Gateway v1.10 (v1.34 to v1.37), with nodes that are Amazon EC2 instances in the same virtual private cloud (VPC) as the proxy. Amazon EKS clusters meet this. For other clusters, see the platform requirements.
  • kubectl, helm (v3), and the AWS CLI.
  • Envoy Gateway v1.10. Controller v1.0.0 is built and tested against it.
  • The VPC ID of your cluster.

The chart and the controller image come from Amazon ECR. The IAM policy and the Envoy Gateway values file come from this repository, so clone the release you install and run the commands from its root:

export VERSION=<release version, for example 1.0.0>
git clone --branch v$VERSION https://github.com/aws/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider.git
cd elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider

The examples also use these variables:

export CLUSTER_NAME=my-cluster
export AWS_REGION=us-west-2
export AWS_ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
export VPC_ID=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --query cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.vpcId --output text)

If your cluster isn't on Amazon EKS, set VPC_ID to the ID of the VPC that your nodes run in.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the controller IAM policy
docs.text:
The sidecar calls the ELB and EC2 APIs. Download k8s/iam-policy.json and replace the ${ClusterName} placeholder with your cluster name:

sed "s/\${ClusterName}/$CLUSTER_NAME/" k8s/iam-policy.json > iam-policy.json

aws iam create-policy \
  --policy-name ELBEnvoyRemoteInfraProviderPolicy \
  --policy-document file://iam-policy.json

The policy scopes write access to resources tagged gateway.elbproxy.aws/managed-by, which the controller adds to everything it creates. The one exception is node security groups. The controller can add ingress rules to security groups tagged kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name>.

docs.title: Step 2: Grant the policy to the Envoy Gateway service account
docs.text:
The sidecar shares the Envoy Gateway pod, so it runs as Envoy Gateway's service account (envoy-gateway in envoy-gateway-system). Give that service account the policy from Step 1.

EKS Pod IdentityIAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) 
aws iam create-role \
  --role-name ELBEnvoyRemoteInfraProviderRole \
  --assume-role-policy-document '{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"Service": "pods.eks.amazonaws.com"},
      "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"]
    }]
  }'

aws iam attach-role-policy \
  --role-name ELBEnvoyRemoteInfraProviderRole \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:policy/ELBEnvoyRemoteInfraProviderPolicy

aws eks create-pod-identity-association \
  --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --namespace envoy-gateway-system \
  --service-account envoy-gateway \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:role/ELBEnvoyRemoteInfraProviderRole

Pod Identity requires the EKS Pod Identity Agent add-on on the cluster. The association is stored in EKS, not on the service account, so it survives Envoy Gateway reinstalls.

Create a role that trusts your cluster's OIDC provider for system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway, and attach the policy from Step 1.

You annotate the service account in Step 4, after Envoy Gateway creates it. Envoy Gateway's Helm chart has no value for service account annotations, so the annotation has to be added with kubectl.

docs.title: Step 3: Install the Helm chart
docs.text:
Envoy Gateway Helm values (default)Webhook

The chart installs only the CRD and the sidecar RBAC. No values are required:

helm install elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider oci://public.ecr.aws/aws-elb-proxy/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-chart \
  --version $VERSION \
  -n elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system --create-namespace

The following table lists the chart values for this option. You set the sidecar's own settings in Envoy Gateway's values instead, in Step 4. For all sidecar flags, see Configurations.

Value Default Description envoyGatewayNamespace envoy-gateway-system Namespace where Envoy Gateway runs. Used for the RBAC binding. If Envoy Gateway runs in another namespace, set it, for example --set envoyGatewayNamespace=<namespace>. rbac.serviceAccountName envoy-gateway Envoy Gateway's service account, which the sidecar runs as.

Install the chart before Envoy Gateway. The webhook only adds the sidecar when a pod is created, so Envoy Gateway pods that already exist won't get it until they restart.

helm install elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider oci://public.ecr.aws/aws-elb-proxy/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-chart \
  --version $VERSION \
  -n elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system --create-namespace \
  --set webhook.enabled=true \
  --set clusterName=$CLUSTER_NAME \
  --set aws.region=$AWS_REGION \
  --set aws.vpcId=$VPC_ID

clusterName is required. Set aws.region and aws.vpcId too: the chart passes them to the sidecar as flags, and the sidecar fails to start if it can't resolve a VPC.

Wait until the webhook is ready before you install Envoy Gateway:

kubectl rollout status deployment/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider \
  -n elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system

Warning

With the default failurePolicy: Fail, Envoy Gateway pods can't be created while no webhook replica is ready, for example during the first install or while a single replica restarts. Keep the webhook running for as long as Envoy Gateway is installed, and run 2 or more replicas (replicaCount) in production.

The following table lists the main chart values for this option. For all sidecar flags, see Configurations.

Value Default Description webhook.enabled false Install the sidecar-injection webhook. Set it to true. clusterName "" Sidecar --cluster-name. Required. aws.region "" Sidecar --aws-region. If empty, the sidecar uses the AWS_REGION environment variable (IRSA sets it). Recommended. aws.vpcId "" Sidecar --aws-vpc-id. Recommended. webhook.sidecar.extraArgs [] Extra flags for the sidecar, for example --default-tags=team=a,env=b. image.repository public.ecr.aws/aws-elb-proxy/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider Image for the webhook and the injected sidecar. image.tag the release tag, for example v1.0.0 Image tag. replicaCount 1 Webhook replicas. webhook.failurePolicy Fail Fail blocks Envoy Gateway pod creation while no webhook replica is ready. Ignore lets the pod start without the sidecar. envoyGatewayNamespace envoy-gateway-system Namespace where Envoy Gateway runs. Used for the RBAC binding and to choose which pods get the sidecar. rbac.serviceAccountName envoy-gateway Envoy Gateway's service account, which the injected sidecar runs as.

docs.title: Step 4: Install Envoy Gateway
docs.text:
Envoy Gateway must send infrastructure to the sidecar over a Unix domain socket instead of creating Envoy deployments in the cluster. This needs a config section in Envoy Gateway's Helm values, with leader election disabled. The values file of the default option already includes it. With the webhook, you write it yourself.

Why leader election must be disabled

Each Envoy Gateway replica sends infrastructure only to the sidecar in its own pod. With Envoy Gateway's leader election on, only the leader sends it, so the other sidecars can act on stale data. With it off, every replica keeps its sidecar up to date. The sidecars then run their own leader election, so only one replica writes to AWS.

Envoy Gateway Helm values (default)Webhook

k8s/envoy-gateway-values.yaml contains the config section and the sidecar: the container, the shared socket volume, and the socket mount on the Envoy Gateway container. Fill in its placeholders:

sed -e "s|<tag>|v$VERSION|" \
    -e "s|<cluster-name>|$CLUSTER_NAME|" \
    -e "s|<region>|$AWS_REGION|" \
    -e "s|<vpc-id>|$VPC_ID|" \
    k8s/envoy-gateway-values.yaml > eg-values.yaml

To set more sidecar flags, such as --default-tags, add them to the sidecar's args in eg-values.yaml. If Envoy Gateway runs in another namespace, also change the ENVOY_GATEWAY_NAMESPACE value.

Save this config section as eg-values.yaml. Don't add the sidecar: the webhook adds it.

config:
  envoyGateway:
    gateway:
      controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/gatewayclass-controller
    provider:
      type: Custom
      custom:
        resource:
          type: Kubernetes
          kubernetes:
            # Required. The sidecar runs its own leader election.
            leaderElection:
              disable: true
        infrastructure:
          type: Remote
          remote:
            service:
              unix:
                # Must match the sidecar's --server-socket-path.
                path: /var/run/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider/server.sock

Then install Envoy Gateway:

helm install eg oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-helm --version v1.10.0 \
  -n envoy-gateway-system --create-namespace \
  -f eg-values.yaml

If the Gateway API CRDs are already installed

If your cluster already has Gateway API CRDs, for example from the AWS Load Balancer Controller, helm install can fail with a CRD conflict. Install the CRDs yourself, then install Envoy Gateway with --skip-crds:

kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts \
  -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.6.1/standard-install.yaml
helm pull oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-crds-helm --version v1.10.0
helm template eg-crds ./gateway-crds-helm-v1.10.0.tgz --set crds.envoyGateway.enabled=true \
  | kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f -
helm install eg oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-helm --version v1.10.0 \
  -n envoy-gateway-system --create-namespace --skip-crds \
  -f eg-values.yaml

Every Gateway API controller in the cluster shares these CRDs, so check that the others support Gateway API v1.6.1 first.

If you use IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA), annotate the service account Envoy Gateway just created, then restart Envoy Gateway so the pod gets credentials:

kubectl annotate serviceaccount envoy-gateway -n envoy-gateway-system \
  eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=arn:aws:iam::$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:role/ELBEnvoyRemoteInfraProviderRole
kubectl rollout restart deployment envoy-gateway -n envoy-gateway-system

Warning

helm uninstall eg deletes the service account and its annotation. After you reinstall Envoy Gateway, run both commands again. Pod Identity doesn't have this problem.

If Envoy Gateway is already installed, upgrade it with the same values and restart it. Use the Envoy Gateway version listed for your controller release. See Upgrading.

helm upgrade eg oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-helm --version v1.10.0 \
  -n envoy-gateway-system -f eg-values.yaml
kubectl rollout restart deployment envoy-gateway -n envoy-gateway-system

docs.title: Step 5: Verify the installation
docs.text:
Check that the Envoy Gateway pod has the sidecar and that both containers are ready:

kubectl get pods -n envoy-gateway-system -l control-plane=envoy-gateway \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{": "}{.spec.initContainers[*].name}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get pods -n envoy-gateway-system -l control-plane=envoy-gateway

The first command should list elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider for each Envoy Gateway pod, and the second should show 2/2 ready. The sidecar is a native sidecar (an init container that keeps running), so it's listed under initContainers.

Check the sidecar logs. A healthy sidecar logs gRPC server listening and Successfully acquired lease (on one replica), with no errors:

kubectl logs -n envoy-gateway-system deployment/envoy-gateway \
  -c elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider

With the webhook, also check that the webhook is running:

kubectl get deployment -n elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system

Next, deploy a Gateway by following Getting Started.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Delete your Gateways first, and wait until they are gone (kubectl get gateways -A). The controller removes their AWS proxies and security groups during this time, so don't uninstall Envoy Gateway before it finishes.

Then delete your ELBProxyConfigurations, while the controller is still running. Each one has a finalizer that only the controller removes, so after you uninstall it they can't be deleted:

kubectl delete elbproxyconfigurations -A --all

Then uninstall:

helm uninstall eg -n envoy-gateway-system
helm uninstall elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider -n elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system

helm uninstall eg leaves the resources that Envoy Gateway's chart creates in its install hooks. Remove them, and delete the namespaces if nothing else runs in them:

kubectl delete mutatingwebhookconfiguration envoy-gateway-topology-injector.envoy-gateway-system
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding,clusterrole eg-gateway-helm-certgen:envoy-gateway-system
kubectl delete namespace envoy-gateway-system elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system

Note

Helm doesn't delete CRDs. To remove the ELBProxyConfiguration CRD, run kubectl delete crd elbproxyconfigurations.gateway.elbproxy.aws.

docs.title: Migrating from in-cluster Envoy
docs.text: This guide moves Gateways from Envoy Gateway's default in-cluster Envoy, with or without a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front, to AWS managed Envoy proxies.

docs.title: Choose a migration approach
docs.text:
The remote infrastructure setting (infrastructure.type: Remote) applies to a whole Envoy Gateway install, not to single Gateways. Once an install is switched to remote, every Gateway it manages goes through elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider. A Gateway without an ELBProxyConfiguration gets no data plane at all.

The AWS proxy also has a new DNS name, so clients must move to a new address either way.

Because of this, use a side-by-side migration: run a second Envoy Gateway install configured as remote, create new Gateways on it, test them, and then move traffic with DNS. Your existing Gateways keep serving traffic until you cut over.

Don't switch an existing install in place

If you switch an install that serves traffic to remote, the Envoy Deployments, Services, and NLBs it created stay in the cluster, but they stop serving traffic. The Service still sends traffic to the port Envoy Gateway used for in-cluster Envoy (for example 10080 for a listener on port 80), and in remote mode Envoy listens on the listener's own port (80). The old Gateways keep their old addresses and still show Programmed. Rolling back the Helm release restores them.

docs.title: Before you migrate
docs.text:
Check your current setup for anything that doesn't carry over. The following table lists what to check.

Check What to do Access logs go to a file or stdout (Envoy Gateway's default) Switch to OpenTelemetry or the Access Log Service (ALS), or set telemetry.accessLog.disable: true. The controller rejects file sinks. You use global rate limiting Not supported. Switch the BackendTrafficPolicy to type: Local, which counts per proxy instance, or plan another alternative before migrating. See Compatibility. EnvoyProxy sets Kubernetes deployment settings (replicas, horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA), resources, pod or Service patches) Not used. AWS scales the proxy. You can drop these settings. Pod networking Pod IPs must be routable in the virtual private cloud (VPC), for example with the Amazon VPC CNI. Envoy Gateway leader election Must be disabled on the remote install. See How it works. You plan to use your own security groups Allow traffic from the proxy to Envoy Gateway pods on TCP 18000, and on TCP 18002 if you use Wasm extensions, and to backend pods, request mirror targets, and ext_authz and ext_proc services on their target ports. Kubernetes and Envoy Gateway versions See Compatibility.

The proxy doesn't pass the client's source IP address to your backends. In X-Forwarded-For and X-Envoy-External-Address, backends see an AWS-owned address, not the client's. If your backends rely on the client IP, for example from NLB client IP preservation or proxy protocol, plan for this before you migrate.

Clients reach the proxy through its DNS name. ELB for Envoy doesn't support static IP addresses yet, such as an NLB's Elastic IP addresses. If your clients or partners allowlist IP addresses, don't migrate yet. See NLB features that aren't supported yet.

docs.title: Mapping NLB settings
docs.text:
If you run an NLB in front of in-cluster Envoy today, usually created by the AWS Load Balancer Controller through annotations on the Envoy Service, map its settings to ELBProxyConfiguration. The following table shows the mapping.

NLB + in-cluster Envoy ELB for Envoy service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme networkConfiguration.ipConfiguration.ipAddressingConfiguration: internet-facing or internal. Changing it later replaces the proxy, which gets a new address. service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ip-address-type: dualstack Set both ipv4Addressability and ipv6Addressability, or EnvoyProxy.spec.ipFamily: DualStack. service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-subnets networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.subnets Subnet discovery tags (kubernetes.io/role/elb, kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb) The same tags. No change needed. loadBalancerSourceRanges spec.ingressCidrs service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-security-groups networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups, or leave unset to let the controller manage them. service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-additional-resource-tags spec.tags, or --default-tags for every proxy. Envoy replicas and HPA Not needed.

See ELBProxyConfiguration for every setting.

docs.title: NLB features that aren't supported yet
docs.text:
ELB for Envoy doesn't support the following NLB features yet, and they have no setting in ELBProxyConfiguration:

  • Static IP addresses, such as Elastic IP addresses on the NLB.
  • AWS PrivateLink, which exposes the NLB as a VPC endpoint service.
  • AWS Global Accelerator, which uses the NLB as an endpoint.

Don't migrate if you depend on these

If your setup uses any of these features with the NLB, don't migrate yet. The new proxy's address can't be used in their place. Keep running in-cluster Envoy with the NLB until ELB for Envoy supports them.

docs.title: Step 1: Install a second Envoy Gateway
docs.text:
Install Envoy Gateway again in a new namespace, configured as a remote infrastructure provider, with its own controllerName. This example uses the namespace envoy-gateway-elb and the controller name gateway.envoyproxy.io/elb-gatewayclass-controller.

Add the sidecar the same way as in the Installation Guide. Use the same $VERSION of the controller as in the Installation Guide. Either way, the new install's config section looks like this:

config:
  envoyGateway:
    gateway:
      # Different from your existing install, so each install only manages its own GatewayClass.
      controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/elb-gatewayclass-controller
    provider:
      type: Custom
      custom:
        resource:
          type: Kubernetes
          kubernetes:
            leaderElection:
              disable: true
        infrastructure:
          type: Remote
          remote:
            service:
              unix:
                path: /var/run/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider/server.sock
Envoy Gateway Helm values (default)Webhook

Fill in k8s/envoy-gateway-values.yaml as in Installation Guide Step 4, then make two changes and save it as eg-elb-values.yaml:

  • Set controllerName to gateway.envoyproxy.io/elb-gatewayclass-controller.
  • Set the sidecar's ENVOY_GATEWAY_NAMESPACE environment variable to envoy-gateway-elb.

Install the controller chart pointed at the new namespace:

helm install elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider oci://public.ecr.aws/aws-elb-proxy/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-chart \
  --version $VERSION \
  -n elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system --create-namespace \
  --set envoyGatewayNamespace=envoy-gateway-elb

Save the config section above as eg-elb-values.yaml. Install the controller chart first, pointed at the new namespace, so the sidecar is injected when the Envoy Gateway pod starts:

helm install elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider oci://public.ecr.aws/aws-elb-proxy/elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-chart \
  --version $VERSION \
  -n elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system --create-namespace \
  --set webhook.enabled=true \
  --set clusterName=$CLUSTER_NAME \
  --set aws.region=$AWS_REGION \
  --set aws.vpcId=$VPC_ID \
  --set envoyGatewayNamespace=envoy-gateway-elb

Grant the controller AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy to the envoy-gateway service account in envoy-gateway-elb, as in Installation Guide Step 2. Then install Envoy Gateway. The CRDs are already installed by your existing install, so skip them:

helm install eg-elb oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-helm --version v1.10.0 \
  -n envoy-gateway-elb --create-namespace --skip-crds \
  -f eg-elb-values.yaml

With IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA), annotate the envoy-gateway service account in envoy-gateway-elb and restart Envoy Gateway, as in Installation Guide Step 4.

Check that the new Envoy Gateway pod has the sidecar, as in Installation Guide Step 5, using the envoy-gateway-elb namespace.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the new GatewayClass
docs.text:
apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: EnvoyProxy
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy
  namespace: envoy-gateway-elb
spec:
  telemetry:
    accessLog:
      disable: true
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy-aws
spec:
  controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/elb-gatewayclass-controller
  parametersRef:
    group: gateway.envoyproxy.io
    kind: EnvoyProxy
    name: elb-proxy
    namespace: envoy-gateway-elb

Copy any other settings from your current EnvoyProxy that still apply, such as metrics sinks, tracing, and bootstrap customization.

docs.title: Step 3: Create new Gateways
docs.text:
For each Gateway you're migrating, create a copy in the same namespace with a new name and gatewayClassName: elb-proxy-aws. Keep the same listeners. Until you attach an ELBProxyConfiguration, the new Gateway shows Programmed=False with reason AddressNotAssigned, and no proxy is created:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: my-gateway-elb
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  gatewayClassName: elb-proxy-aws
  listeners:
    # Same listeners as my-gateway
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80

Then attach an ELBProxyConfiguration, using the settings you mapped above:

apiVersion: gateway.elbproxy.aws/v1alpha1
kind: ELBProxyConfiguration
metadata:
  name: my-gateway-elb
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      name: my-gateway-elb
  roleArn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-proxy-role
  networkConfiguration:
    ipConfiguration:
      ipAddressingConfiguration:
        ipv4Addressability: internet-facing
        ipv6Addressability: "off"

Tip

To apply one configuration to every migrated Gateway, target the GatewayClass instead, from an ELBProxyConfiguration in envoy-gateway-elb.

docs.title: Step 4: Attach your routes to both Gateways
docs.text:
Add the new Gateway to each route's parentRefs, so the old and new Gateways serve the same routes during the migration:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: my-route
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: my-gateway
    - name: my-gateway-elb
  rules:
    # unchanged

Its own Envoy Gateway install handles each Gateway, so the existing Gateway keeps serving traffic unchanged.

docs.title: Step 5: Test the new Gateway
docs.text:
Wait for the new Gateway to be programmed, and get its address:

kubectl wait gateway/my-gateway-elb -n my-app --for=condition=Programmed --timeout=15m
export NEW_HOST=$(kubectl get gateway my-gateway-elb -n my-app \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[0].value}')

Send test requests directly to the new address, with the Host header your routes expect:

curl -i -H "Host: www.example.com" http://$NEW_HOST/

Check routing, TLS, headers, and backend behavior the same way you test the current Gateway. If something fails, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Step 6: Shift traffic
docs.text:
The new Gateway has a new address, so you move clients to it. How you do that depends on how clients reach your Gateways today.

Check how clients connect before you shift

If clients use your own hostname, such as api.example.com, you can shift traffic by changing DNS records. If clients call the old address directly, such as the NLB's DNS name, you can't shift traffic without updating every client. Plan for this before you migrate.

The exact steps depend on your DNS provider and traffic management tooling. Look for the ability to shift traffic gradually and to roll back quickly. For example, with Amazon Route 53 weighted records:

  1. Create a weighted CNAME record for your hostname that points at the old address, and a second one that points at $NEW_HOST, with a small weight on the new one. A CNAME record can't be used at the zone apex.
  2. Watch error rates and latency on both.
  3. Increase the weight on the new address until it takes all traffic.

Keep the old Gateway running until the old address gets no traffic.

To roll back, move the DNS weight back to the old address. The old Gateway is unchanged until you delete it.

docs.title: Step 7: Clean up
docs.text:
When the old Gateways get no traffic:

  1. Remove the old Gateway from each route's parentRefs.
  2. Delete the old Gateways. If an NLB was in front, deleting the old Envoy deployment removes its Service and the NLB.
  3. When no Gateways are left on the old install, uninstall it, and delete its GatewayClass and EnvoyProxy.
  4. helm uninstall leaves some Envoy Gateway resources behind: the certgen ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding, and the envoy-gateway-topology-injector MutatingWebhookConfiguration, each named for the old release or namespace. Delete them.

docs.title: Security groups
docs.text:
The proxy runs in your virtual private cloud (VPC) and needs two kinds of network access: clients reaching its listeners, and the proxy reaching Envoy Gateway and your pods. By default, the controller manages the security groups for both. You can also bring your own.

The following table compares the two modes.

Mode Set by The controller manages Controller-managed (default) vpcConfiguration.securityGroups unset A frontend security group per proxy, a shared backend security group, and rules on your node security groups Your own vpcConfiguration.securityGroups set Nothing. You manage every rule.

docs.title: Controller-managed security groups
docs.text: clients --listener ports--> [frontend SG] proxy [backend SG] --18000, 18002, backend ports--> [node SG] Envoy Gateway pods, backend pods

docs.title: Frontend security group
docs.text:
One per proxy: per Gateway, or per GatewayClass for merged gateways. It allows inbound traffic to the proxy's listeners:

  • One rule per listener port and protocol. TCP for TCP-based listeners and UDP for UDPRoute listeners. For an HTTP/3 listener, the HTTPS port also gets a UDP rule for QUIC.
  • Sources:
    • spec.ingressCidrs. IPv6 CIDRs are dropped when the proxy has IPv6 off.
    • If ingressCidrs is unset: 0.0.0.0/0, plus ::/0 when the proxy has IPv6 enabled. For an internal proxy, that means anyone in the VPC or connected networks.
    • spec.ingressPrefixLists, in addition to the CIDRs.
spec:
  ingressCidrs:
    - 10.0.0.0/8
  ingressPrefixLists:
    - pl-0123456789abcdef0

When you change ingressCidrs, ingressPrefixLists, or the Gateway's listeners, the controller updates the rules in place. The security group and the proxy stay the same.

Rules you add by hand are removed

The controller keeps the frontend security group's inbound rules exactly in sync with the listeners and sources above, and removes any other rule on the next reconcile. To open more ports, such as 19001 for Prometheus, bring your own security groups.

The controller doesn't manage outbound rules. A new security group allows all outbound traffic.

docs.title: Backend security group
docs.text:
One per controller installation (cluster name and controller namespace), attached to every proxy that installation manages. It has no rules of its own. It's the source for the node security group rules below, so one set of node rules covers every proxy.

The controller creates it when the first managed proxy needs it, and deletes it when no Gateway does.

docs.title: Node security group rules
docs.text:
The controller adds inbound rules to your node security groups, with the backend security group as the source:

  • TCP 18000, so the proxy can get its configuration from Envoy Gateway over xDS.
  • TCP 18002, so the proxy can download Wasm modules from Envoy Gateway.
  • Every backend target port, with its protocol, that the Gateways this installation manages send traffic to: route backends, request mirror targets, and the ext_authz and ext_proc services of your SecurityPolicy and EnvoyExtensionPolicy resources. The ports for mirror targets and policy services use TCP.

The controller adds the two Envoy Gateway ports as soon as a Gateway exists, even before a route does, and removes all of these rules when the last Gateway is deleted. It labels each rule with its installation and adds or removes only its own rules, so multiple installations and other tools can share a node security group.

Which node security groups. For each Ready EC2 node, the controller uses the security group on the node's primary network interface. If that interface has several security groups, it uses the one tagged kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name>, and there must be exactly one. The controller AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy only allows rule changes on security groups with that tag, so the node security group needs it. The EKS cluster security group has it by default. When the last Gateway is deleted, the controller removes its rules from every security group in the VPC that has this tag.

Pods with their own security groups

The controller adds rules only to node security groups. If your pods have their own security groups, for example with security groups for pods or with custom networking on the Amazon VPC CNI, the controller doesn't change those groups, and the node security group rules above don't apply to the pods' network interfaces. Add the following inbound rules yourself, with the backend security group as the source, or your own security groups if you bring your own:

  • TCP 18000 on the security group of the Envoy Gateway pods, and TCP 18002 if you use Wasm extensions.
  • Each backend target port on the security group of the backend pods.

Without them, the proxy gets no configuration from Envoy Gateway, or requests to your backends fail. Neither shows up as an error in the cluster. To find the backend security group, see Find the security groups.

docs.title: Find the security groups
docs.text:
# Frontend SG of a Gateway
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --filters Name=tag:gateway.elbproxy.aws/cluster,Values=$CLUSTER_NAME \
            Name=tag:gateway.elbproxy.aws/stack,Values=<gateway-namespace>/<gateway-name> \
            Name=tag:gateway.elbproxy.aws/resource,Values=FrontendSecurityGroup \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[].GroupId' --output text

# Backend SG
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --filters Name=tag:gateway.elbproxy.aws/cluster,Values=$CLUSTER_NAME \
            Name=tag:gateway.elbproxy.aws/resource,Values=BackendSecurityGroup \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[].[GroupId,GroupName]' --output text

Frontend security groups are named elbproxy-<cluster>-<namespace>-<gateway>-<hash>, and the backend security group elbproxy-backend-<cluster>-<hash>, with each part shortened.

docs.title: Bring your own security groups
docs.text:
List your security groups in the ELBProxyConfiguration:

spec:
  networkConfiguration:
    vpcConfiguration:
      securityGroups:
        - securityGroupId: sg-0123456789abcdef0

The proxy then uses exactly these security groups, and the controller:

  • doesn't create a frontend or backend security group,
  • doesn't add node security group rules,
  • never changes or deletes your security groups,
  • ignores ingressCidrs and ingressPrefixLists, and logs that it did.

You must allow the access in the following table yourself.

Direction Port Between Inbound to the proxy Each listener port From your clients, on your security groups Inbound to your nodes TCP 18000 From your security groups to the Envoy Gateway pods Inbound to your nodes TCP 18002 From your security groups to the Envoy Gateway pods, if you use Wasm extensions Inbound to your nodes Each backend target port From your security groups to the backend pods, and to any request mirror, ext_authz, or ext_proc services Outbound from the proxy All of the above, plus any telemetry On your security groups

Warning

Without the 18000 rule, the proxy gets no configuration from Envoy Gateway. Without the 18002 rule, the proxy can't download Wasm modules. Without the backend port rules, requests fail. Neither shows up as an error in the cluster.

When you change the list, the controller replaces the proxy's security groups in place.

docs.title: Switch between modes
docs.text:
Controller-managed to your own. In one reconcile, the controller switches the proxy to your security groups. It then deletes its old frontend security group. The proxy no longer has the backend security group, so the controller's node rules stop applying to it. Before switching, make sure your node security groups allow your security groups on TCP 18000 and the backend ports. Otherwise, the proxy loses its configuration and can't reach your pods.

Your own to controller-managed. Remove securityGroups. The controller creates the frontend and backend security groups, adds the node rules, and switches the proxy to them. Your security groups are detached but not changed or deleted.

docs.title: Telemetry ports
docs.text:
Ports for logs and metrics aren't opened in either mode:

  • To a collector in the cluster (OpenTelemetry on 4317): allow it on your node security group from the backend security group, or from your own security groups.
  • To the proxy's Prometheus port 19001: needs your own security groups, because the controller removes extra rules from the frontend security group.

See Observability.

docs.title: Subnet discovery
docs.text: This page explains how the controller chooses the subnets for each proxy, and how to control that choice. Each proxy runs in at least two subnets, one for each Availability Zone, in the cluster's virtual private cloud (VPC). You can list the subnets yourself in the ELBProxyConfiguration, or let the controller discover them.

docs.title: How the controller picks subnets
docs.text:
For each proxy, the controller uses the first of these that applies:

  1. Subnets in the spec. If spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.subnets is set, it uses exactly those. See Specify subnets.
  2. The existing proxy's subnets. If the proxy already exists, it keeps the subnets the proxy has now. Discovery doesn't run again, so later tag changes don't move an existing proxy.
  3. Discovery. Otherwise, it discovers subnets as described below.

docs.title: Candidate subnets
docs.text:
The controller looks for subnets in the cluster's VPC with the role tag that matches the proxy's addressability. The following table shows each role tag.

Addressability Role tag internet-facing kubernetes.io/role/elb internal kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb

The tag's value must be 1 or empty. These are the same tags the AWS Load Balancer Controller uses, so subnets already tagged for it work without changes.

Addressability comes from ipv4Addressability. For an IPv6-only proxy (ipv4Addressability: off), it comes from ipv6Addressability instead. See Addressability for the defaults.

If no subnet has the role tag, the controller falls back to route tables. A subnet whose route table has a route to an internet gateway counts as public, and is a candidate for internet-facing proxies. Any other subnet counts as private, and is a candidate for internal proxies. A subnet without its own route table uses the VPC's main route table.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
From the candidates, the controller skips a subnet if:

  • It's tagged kubernetes.io/cluster/<name> only for other clusters. Subnets with no cluster tag, or with this cluster's tag, are kept.
  • It has fewer than 8 available IP addresses.
  • The proxy has IPv6 enabled and the subnet has no associated IPv6 CIDR block.

docs.title: Final selection
docs.text:
The controller then picks one subnet per Availability Zone:

  • A subnet tagged kubernetes.io/cluster/<this cluster> wins over an untagged one.
  • Otherwise, the subnet with the lowest subnet ID wins.

Subnets in Local Zones, Wavelength Zones, and Outposts are dropped. The result must have at least two subnets. If it doesn't, the Gateway gets a FailedDeployModel event. If no subnet is eligible, the event says how many subnets were skipped, and why. If only one remains, it says the count is below the minimum of two. See FailedDeployModel errors.

docs.title: Tag your subnets
docs.text:
Tag at least two subnets, in different Availability Zones, for each kind of proxy you create:

# Subnets for internet-facing proxies
aws ec2 create-tags --resources subnet-0123456789abcdef0 subnet-0fedcba9876543210 \
  --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/elb,Value=1

# Subnets for internal proxies
aws ec2 create-tags --resources subnet-0aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa subnet-0bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb \
  --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb,Value=1

If several clusters share the VPC, also tag each subnet kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name>=shared for the clusters that may use it. The controller skips a subnet tagged only for other clusters.

docs.title: Specify subnets
docs.text:
To choose subnets yourself, list them in the ELBProxyConfiguration:

spec:
  networkConfiguration:
    vpcConfiguration:
      subnets:
        - subnetId: subnet-0123456789abcdef0
        - subnetId: subnet-0fedcba9876543210

The list must have:

  • At least two subnets, each in a different Availability Zone.
  • Only standard Availability Zones. A subnet in a Local Zone, Wavelength Zone, or Outpost is rejected.
  • An associated IPv6 CIDR block on every subnet, when the proxy has IPv6 enabled.

subnetId also accepts a subnet's Name tag value instead of its ID. A name has to match a subnet in the cluster's VPC. The controller doesn't check the VPC for IDs, so list only subnets from the cluster's VPC.

Role tags, cluster tags, and free IP addresses aren't checked for subnets you list. Make sure they suit the proxy's addressability: for example, internet-facing proxies need public subnets.

docs.title: Change subnets on an existing proxy
docs.text:
• Edit subnets: the controller updates the proxy's subnets in place. The proxy and its address stay the same.
  • Remove subnets: the proxy keeps the subnets it has now. Discovery doesn't run again.
  • Move a discovered proxy to other subnets: retagging subnets has no effect on an existing proxy. List the new subnets in subnets instead.
  • Change addressability: a change to ipConfiguration, or to the EnvoyProxy's ipFamily when ipConfiguration is unset, replaces the proxy, and the new proxy gets a new address. Because the role tag depends on addressability, list subnets explicitly when you make this change. This ensures the new proxy lands in subnets that suit it.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This walkthrough deploys an echo application and exposes it through a Gateway that runs on an AWS managed Envoy proxy.

You create:

  1. An EnvoyProxy and a GatewayClass that Envoy Gateway uses for this walkthrough.
  2. An echo backend.
  3. A Gateway and an HTTPRoute.
  4. An ELBProxyConfiguration that tells the controller to create an AWS proxy for the Gateway.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Costs

This walkthrough creates AWS resources that can incur charges: an ELB for Envoy proxy, plus the network interfaces and security groups that the controller creates in your virtual private cloud (VPC). Follow Clean up when you finish to avoid ongoing charges.

  • The controller and Envoy Gateway are installed. See the Installation Guide.
  • At least two public subnets in different Availability Zones. For an internet-facing proxy, the controller looks for subnets tagged kubernetes.io/role/elb (value 1 or empty). If no subnet has the tag, it uses subnets with a route to an internet gateway. See Subnet discovery.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for the proxy, set as spec.roleArn. If you don't have one, create it in Create the proxy role.

docs.title: Create the proxy role
docs.text:
Creating a proxy requires a proxy role, which you set as spec.roleArn. The proxy uses this role to publish its logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and for the permissions that code in your Envoy configuration, such as filters and extensions, needs when it calls AWS services. To let ELB for Envoy publish the proxy's logs, the role needs at least the following permissions:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "logs:CreateLogGroup",
        "logs:CreateLogStream",
        "logs:PutLogEvents"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:*:logs:*:*:log-group:/aws/elb-proxy/*",
        "arn:*:logs:*:*:log-group:/aws/elb-proxy/*:log-stream:*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The trust policy of the role must allow elasticloadbalancing.amazonaws.com to assume it, so that ELB for Envoy can give the role's credentials to your proxy:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Service": "elasticloadbalancing.amazonaws.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}

To create the role with the AWS CLI, save the two policies as trust-policy.json and logs-policy.json, then run:

aws iam create-role --role-name my-proxy-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json

aws iam put-role-policy --role-name my-proxy-role \
  --policy-name ELBProxyEnvoyLogs \
  --policy-document file://logs-policy.json

export PROXY_ROLE_ARN=$(aws iam get-role --role-name my-proxy-role \
  --query Role.Arn --output text)

If you already have a role, set PROXY_ROLE_ARN to its ARN instead:

export PROXY_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-proxy-role

docs.title: Step 1: Create the EnvoyProxy and GatewayClass
docs.text:
The GatewayClass belongs to Envoy Gateway, not to this controller. It points at an EnvoyProxy that disables access logging.

Disable access logging or use a network sink

Envoy Gateway's default access log writes to /dev/stdout, which doesn't exist on the managed proxy. The controller rejects a Gateway whose EnvoyProxy uses a file sink or leaves access logging unset. Set telemetry.accessLog.disable: true, or use an OpenTelemetry or ALS sink.

apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: EnvoyProxy
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy
  namespace: envoy-gateway-system
spec:
  ipFamily: IPv4
  telemetry:
    accessLog:
      disable: true
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy-aws
spec:
  controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/gatewayclass-controller
  parametersRef:
    group: gateway.envoyproxy.io
    kind: EnvoyProxy
    name: elb-proxy
    namespace: envoy-gateway-system

Save this as gatewayclass.yaml and apply it:

kubectl apply -f gatewayclass.yaml

docs.title: Step 2: Deploy the echo backend
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: echo
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: echo
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: echo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: echo
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: echo
          image: registry.k8s.io/gateway-api/echo-basic:v1.5.1
          env:
            - name: POD_NAME
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.name
            - name: NAMESPACE
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.namespace
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: echo
spec:
  selector:
    app: echo
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 3000

Save this as echo.yaml and apply it:

kubectl apply -f echo.yaml

docs.title: Step 3: Create the Gateway and HTTPRoute
docs.text:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: echo-gateway
  namespace: echo
spec:
  gatewayClassName: elb-proxy-aws
  listeners:
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: echo
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: echo-gateway
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /
      backendRefs:
        - name: echo
          port: 8080

Save this as gateway.yaml and apply it:

kubectl apply -f gateway.yaml

The Gateway doesn't have an address yet. The controller only creates an AWS proxy for a Gateway that has an ELBProxyConfiguration attached.

docs.title: Step 4: Attach an ELBProxyConfiguration
docs.text:
Create the ELBProxyConfiguration in the same namespace as the Gateway:

apiVersion: gateway.elbproxy.aws/v1alpha1
kind: ELBProxyConfiguration
metadata:
  name: echo-proxy
  namespace: echo
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      name: echo-gateway
  roleArn: ${PROXY_ROLE_ARN}
  networkConfiguration:
    ipConfiguration:
      ipAddressingConfiguration:
        ipv4Addressability: internet-facing
        ipv6Addressability: "off"

Save this as proxy.yaml and apply it, substituting the role Amazon Resource Name (ARN):

envsubst < proxy.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

This example sets internet-facing so you can reach the proxy from your machine. If you leave ipConfiguration unset, the proxy is internal and only reachable from inside the VPC.

If you don't set subnets, the controller discovers them from the kubernetes.io/role/elb tag. To pick subnets yourself, set spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.subnets with at least two subnets in different Availability Zones.

By default, the controller creates a security group that allows traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 (plus ::/0 with IPv6) on the listener ports. To restrict it, set spec.ingressCidrs.

docs.title: Step 5: Wait for the proxy
docs.text:
Check that the ELBProxyConfiguration is accepted:

kubectl get elbproxyconfiguration echo-proxy -n echo \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Accepted")].status}{"\n"}'

The output should be True.

Provisioning the AWS proxy takes several minutes. The controller checks the proxy's status about every 2 minutes, so the Gateway can become Programmed a little after the proxy is active. Wait for the Gateway to become Programmed:

kubectl wait gateway/echo-gateway -n echo \
  --for=condition=Programmed --timeout=15m

Watch the Gateway's events for errors. The controller emits no event while the proxy is being created:

kubectl describe gateway echo-gateway -n echo

FailedDeployModel means the controller couldn't create or update the proxy. The event message has the error. SuccessfullyReconciled means the controller applied the configuration; it doesn't mean the proxy is active.

To see the proxy's own state, check the ELBProxyConfiguration. Its Programmed condition shows Pending while the proxy is being created:

kubectl get elbproxyconfiguration echo-proxy -n echo \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.proxies[0].conditions[?(@.type=="Programmed")].reason}{": "}{.status.proxies[0].conditions[?(@.type=="Programmed")].message}{"\n"}'

If it shows ActionRequired or CreateFailed, see Check the proxy's status.

docs.title: Step 6: Send a request
docs.text:
The Gateway's address is the proxy's DNS name:

export GATEWAY_HOST=$(kubectl get gateway echo-gateway -n echo \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[0].value}')

curl -i http://$GATEWAY_HOST/

The echo server replies with JSON that includes the pod name and namespace. The DNS name can take a few minutes to resolve after the proxy is created.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• TLS certificates: serve HTTPS with cert-manager or ACM.
  • Observability: send the proxy's metrics to your telemetry stack.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Delete the Gateway first, so the controller removes the AWS proxy and the security groups it created. Then delete the rest:

kubectl delete -f gateway.yaml
kubectl delete -f proxy.yaml
kubectl delete -f echo.yaml
kubectl delete -f gatewayclass.yaml

The controller removes the AWS proxy and the security groups in the background, which takes a few minutes. Keep the controller running until it finishes.

When the proxy is gone, delete the proxy role if you created it in Create the proxy role:

aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name my-proxy-role --policy-name ELBProxyEnvoyLogs
aws iam delete-role --role-name my-proxy-role

docs.title: Merged Gateways
docs.text:
This walkthrough runs two Gateways, owned by two teams, on one AWS managed proxy. With Envoy Gateway's merged gateways mode, all Gateways in a GatewayClass share a proxy and its address. The proxy tells the Gateways apart by their listener hostnames.

You create:

  1. An EnvoyProxy with mergeGateways: true, and a GatewayClass that uses it.
  2. An ELBProxyConfiguration for the whole class.
  3. For each team, a namespace with an echo backend, a Gateway, and an HTTPRoute.

For the concepts, see Merged gateways.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Costs

This walkthrough creates AWS resources that can incur charges: one ELB for Envoy proxy, plus the network interfaces and security groups that the controller creates in your virtual private cloud (VPC). Delete them when you finish. See Clean up.

Complete the prerequisites in Getting Started: the controller and Envoy Gateway installed, subnets, and the proxy role.

export PROXY_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-proxy-role

docs.title: Step 1: Create the EnvoyProxy and GatewayClass
docs.text:
Set mergeGateways: true on the EnvoyProxy. A merged class needs its own EnvoyProxy, so don't reuse the one from Getting Started.

apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: EnvoyProxy
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy-merged
  namespace: envoy-gateway-system
spec:
  mergeGateways: true
  ipFamily: IPv4
  telemetry:
    accessLog:
      disable: true
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy-aws-merged
spec:
  controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/gatewayclass-controller
  parametersRef:
    group: gateway.envoyproxy.io
    kind: EnvoyProxy
    name: elb-proxy-merged
    namespace: envoy-gateway-system

Save this as merged-gatewayclass.yaml and apply it:

kubectl apply -f merged-gatewayclass.yaml

docs.title: Step 2: Attach an ELBProxyConfiguration to the class
docs.text:
In merged mode, only a configuration that targets the GatewayClass applies. Create it in the Envoy Gateway namespace, not in a team's namespace:

apiVersion: gateway.elbproxy.aws/v1alpha1
kind: ELBProxyConfiguration
metadata:
  name: merged-proxy
  namespace: envoy-gateway-system
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: GatewayClass
      name: elb-proxy-aws-merged
  roleArn: ${PROXY_ROLE_ARN}
  networkConfiguration:
    ipConfiguration:
      ipAddressingConfiguration:
        ipv4Addressability: internet-facing
        ipv6Addressability: "off"

Save this as merged-proxy.yaml and apply it, substituting the role Amazon Resource Name (ARN):

envsubst < merged-proxy.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

docs.title: Step 3: Deploy each team's backend, Gateway, and route
docs.text:
Each team gets a namespace, an echo backend, a Gateway with its own hostname, and a route. The two Gateways use the same port. The hostnames keep them apart.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: echo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: echo
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: echo
          image: registry.k8s.io/gateway-api/echo-basic:v1.5.1
          env:
            - name: POD_NAME
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.name
            - name: NAMESPACE
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.namespace
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  selector:
    app: echo
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: team-a
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  gatewayClassName: elb-proxy-aws-merged
  listeners:
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
      hostname: a.example.com
      allowedRoutes:
