        namespaces:
          from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: team-a
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: echo
          port: 8080

Save this as team-a.yaml. Make a copy for the second team, replacing team-a with team-b and a.example.com with b.example.com, and save it as team-b.yaml:

sed -e 's/team-a/team-b/g' -e 's/a\.example\.com/b.example.com/g' team-a.yaml > team-b.yaml
kubectl apply -f team-a.yaml -f team-b.yaml

docs.title: Step 4: Wait for the proxy
docs.text:
Provisioning the AWS proxy takes several minutes. Wait for both Gateways to become Programmed:

kubectl wait gateway/team-a -n team-a --for=condition=Programmed --timeout=15m
kubectl wait gateway/team-b -n team-b --for=condition=Programmed --timeout=15m

There is one proxy for the class, so one entry in the configuration's status:

kubectl get elbproxyconfiguration merged-proxy -n envoy-gateway-system \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.proxies[*]}{.gatewayRef.name}{": "}{.conditions[?(@.type=="Programmed")].message}{"\n"}{end}'

Both Gateways report the same address, which is the proxy's DNS name:

kubectl get gateway -A \
  -o 'custom-columns=NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,ADDRESS:.status.addresses[0].value'

docs.title: Step 5: Send requests
docs.text:
Send a request to the shared address with each team's hostname. The Host header chooses the Gateway, and each reply names the team's namespace:

export GATEWAY_HOST=$(kubectl get gateway team-a -n team-a \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[0].value}')
curl -s -H "Host: a.example.com" http://$GATEWAY_HOST/ | grep '"namespace"'
curl -s -H "Host: b.example.com" http://$GATEWAY_HOST/ | grep '"namespace"'

The first command prints "namespace": "team-a" and the second prints "namespace": "team-b". The DNS name can take a few minutes to resolve after the proxy is created.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• ELBProxyConfiguration: every setting for the proxy, including which configuration applies in merged mode.
  • Security groups: how the controller opens the listener ports of all the Gateways in the class.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Delete the Gateways first, so the controller removes the AWS proxy and the security groups it created. Then delete the rest:

kubectl delete -f team-a.yaml -f team-b.yaml
kubectl delete -f merged-proxy.yaml
kubectl delete -f merged-gatewayclass.yaml

The controller removes the AWS proxy and the security groups in the background, which takes a few minutes. Keep the controller running until it finishes.

docs.title: AWS integrations
docs.text:
This page covers two AWS services that you can connect to a proxy through its ELBProxyConfiguration:

  • AWS WAF: filter the proxy's HTTP traffic with your own web ACL.
  • Customer managed KMS keys: encrypt the proxy's configuration with your own AWS KMS key.

Both are off by default. Each one needs extra permissions in the controller IAM policy (k8s/iam-policy.json). If you don't use a service, you can remove its statements from the policy.

docs.title: AWS WAF
docs.text: A proxy has no AWS WAF protection by default. To protect it, you create your own web ACL in AWS WAF and give its ARN to the proxy. The ELB for Envoy service never creates, changes, or deletes a web ACL. It only records which web ACL is associated with the proxy.

docs.title: Set a web ACL when you create the proxy
docs.text:
Set the web ACL's ARN in the waf.web_acl_arn attribute:

spec:
  attributes:
    - key: waf.web_acl_arn
      value: arn:aws:wafv2:us-west-2:111122223333:regional/webacl/my-acl/a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-EXAMPLE11111

The web ACL must be a regional web ACL in the same Region as the proxy. When the controller creates the proxy, the service associates the web ACL during the create call. If the ARN is wrong, the web ACL doesn't exist, or the controller lacks permission, the proxy isn't created, and the Gateway gets a FailedDeployModel event with the error.

The service applies the web ACL's rules to requests before they reach your backends. A request that a rule blocks gets 403 Forbidden from the proxy.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The service associates the web ACL with the controller's credentials, so the controller IAM policy needs these two statements:

{
    "Sid": "WAFAssociateWebACL",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "wafv2:AssociateWebACL",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:wafv2:*:*:regional/webacl/*/*"
},
{
    "Sid": "ELBProxyWafAssociation",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": [
        "elasticloadbalancing:CreateProxyWafAssociation",
        "elasticloadbalancing:DeleteProxyWafAssociation",
        "elasticloadbalancing:GetProxyWafAssociation",
        "elasticloadbalancing:ListProxyWafAssociations"
    ],
    "Resource": "*"
}
  • WAFAssociateWebACL lets the controller use a web ACL. AWS WAF checks wafv2:AssociateWebACL on the web ACL itself, the same way it does when you protect an Application Load Balancer. The resource matches any regional web ACL. To allow only specific web ACLs, replace regional/webacl/*/* with their names, for example regional/webacl/my-acl/*.
  • ELBProxyWafAssociation lets the controller attach a web ACL to the proxy, on the ELB for Envoy side.

Without these statements, creating a proxy that sets waf.web_acl_arn fails with is not authorized to perform: wafv2:AssociateWebACL or elasticloadbalancing:CreateProxyWafAssociation. A proxy that doesn't set it doesn't need them.

docs.title: Change or remove the web ACL
docs.text:
The service doesn't change waf.web_acl_arn with an attribute update. To change or remove the web ACL on an existing proxy, call AWS WAF with the proxy's ARN, then update spec.attributes to match:

  1. Get the proxy ARN: 
    kubectl get elbproxyconfiguration <name> -n <namespace> \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.proxies[0].proxyArn}{"\n"}'
  2. Change or remove the web ACL: 
    # Use a different web ACL. The new one replaces the old one.
aws wafv2 associate-web-acl --web-acl-arn <new-web-acl-arn> --resource-arn <proxy-arn>

# Remove WAF protection.
aws wafv2 disassociate-web-acl --resource-arn <proxy-arn>
  3. If spec.attributes has waf.web_acl_arn, set it to the new ARN, or remove the entry. If the spec doesn't have the key, you don't need to change anything.

You run these commands with your own credentials, so you need wafv2:AssociateWebACL or wafv2:DisassociateWebACL. The controller doesn't need them for this.

Don't change waf.web_acl_arn in the spec only

If the value in the spec doesn't match the web ACL on the proxy, the controller stops with the error attribute "waf.web_acl_arn" is read-only, and the Gateway gets a FailedDeployModel event. Until the spec matches again, the controller doesn't apply the proxy's other changes either, such as network and Envoy configuration updates. It also retries about twice a second, and each retry calls the ELB for Envoy API, so fix the mismatch quickly.

docs.title: Check which web ACL protects a proxy
docs.text:
aws wafv2 get-web-acl-for-resource --resource-arn <proxy-arn> --query 'WebACL.Name'

To list the proxies that use a web ACL, pass --resource-type ELB_PROXY. Without it, AWS WAF lists only Application Load Balancers:

aws wafv2 list-resources-for-web-acl --web-acl-arn <web-acl-arn> --resource-type ELB_PROXY

docs.title: Deleting a proxy or a web ACL
docs.text: Deleting the Gateway deletes the proxy and its association. Your web ACL stays in your account. AWS WAF doesn't delete a web ACL that is still associated with a proxy, so remove it from the proxy first.

docs.title: When AWS WAF is unavailable
docs.text: By default, the proxy blocks requests when it can't reach AWS WAF. To let them through instead, set waf.fail_open.enabled to true. Unlike waf.web_acl_arn, you can change this attribute at any time in spec.attributes.

docs.title: Customer managed KMS keys
docs.text:
The service stores each proxy's configuration encrypted. By default, it uses a key that the service owns. To use your own AWS KMS key instead, set its ARN in spec.customerKmsKeyArn:

spec:
  customerKmsKeyArn: arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:111122223333:key/1234abcd-12ab-34cd-56ef-1234567890ab

The key must be a symmetric encryption key (SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT, usage ENCRYPT_DECRYPT), enabled, and in the same Region as the proxy. Otherwise the service rejects it, and the Gateway gets a FailedDeployModel event with the error.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The service encrypts the configuration under your key with the controller's credentials, so the controller IAM policy needs these two statements:

{
    "Sid": "CustomerKmsDescribe",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "kms:DescribeKey",
    "Resource": "*"
},
{
    "Sid": "CustomerKmsCryptoOps",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": [
        "kms:GenerateDataKey",
        "kms:Decrypt"
    ],
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {
        "StringLike": {
            "kms:EncryptionContext:aws:elasticloadbalancing:proxy-arn": "arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:*:*:proxy/*"
        }
    }
}
  • CustomerKmsDescribe lets the service check that the key is usable before it encrypts with it.
  • CustomerKmsCryptoOps lets the service create and read the data keys that encrypt the configuration. The condition limits both actions to requests whose encryption context names a proxy ARN, which is how the service calls them.

To allow only your own keys, replace "Resource": "*" with their ARNs. The key policy must also allow the controller's role to use the key, unless it delegates access to IAM policies.

docs.title: Change the key
docs.text:
When you change customerKmsKeyArn, the controller sends the proxy's whole configuration again with the new key, and the service re-encrypts it. The proxy isn't replaced, but Envoy restarts with the re-encrypted configuration.

Removing customerKmsKeyArn from a proxy that uses your key asks the service to go back to its own key. The service might not support this yet. If it rejects the change, the Gateway gets a FailedDeployModel event, and the proxy keeps your key.

docs.title: If the service loses access to the key
docs.text: If you disable the key, schedule it for deletion, or remove the controller's access, the service can't read the proxy's configuration. The proxy's status in the ELBProxyConfiguration then shows ActionRequired, with the reason from AWS. See Check the proxy's status. Restore access to the key to fix it.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
The proxy runs in your virtual private cloud (VPC), outside the cluster. Its logs and metrics don't appear in the cluster on their own: the proxy has to send them over the network to a collector you run, or your scraper has to reach the proxy. This page covers both, and the network setup each needs.

You configure telemetry as you normally do in Envoy Gateway, in the EnvoyProxy that your GatewayClass references, for example elb-proxy from Getting Started.

The following table lists the telemetry signals and how to configure each one.

Signal How Notes Access logs OpenTelemetry or Access Log Service (ALS) sink in telemetry.accessLog File sinks, including Envoy Gateway's default /dev/stdout, don't work. See Access logs. Metrics, pushed OpenTelemetry sink in telemetry.metrics.sinks Recommended for metrics. See Push metrics. Metrics, pulled Prometheus endpoint on the proxy, port 19001 Needs your own security groups. See Pull metrics.

docs.title: How the proxy reaches your collector
docs.text:
The proxy connects to a collector in your VPC the same way it connects to your backend pods: directly, by IP. The source of that traffic depends on how the proxy's security groups are set up.

Controller-managed security groups (default). Every proxy the controller creates in the cluster has one shared backend security group. That's the source of the proxy's traffic to your pods. The controller adds rules on your node security group that allow it in, but only for Envoy Gateway's xDS port (18000) and its Wasm module port (18002), which it opens while any Gateway is active, and the ports your Gateways send traffic to, such as your backends and ext_authz or ext_proc services. It never opens a telemetry port, so you add that rule yourself.

Find the backend security group:

export BACKEND_SG=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --filters Name=tag:gateway.elbproxy.aws/cluster,Values=$CLUSTER_NAME \
            Name=tag:gateway.elbproxy.aws/resource,Values=BackendSecurityGroup \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[].GroupId' --output text)

Your own security groups. If you set spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups, there's no backend security group and the controller doesn't manage any rules. Use your security groups as the source instead.

See Security groups for how both modes work.

Warning

If this rule is missing, the proxy can't connect to the collector, and nothing in the cluster reports it. Envoy Gateway and the Gateway both look healthy, and no data arrives. A connection that is already open keeps working, so the problem can appear later, for example after the collector restarts.

docs.title: Access logs
docs.text:
Access logs are sent with an OpenTelemetry sink to a collector in the cluster, which forwards them to wherever you store logs, such as CloudWatch Logs or Loki.

proxy (Envoy) --OTLP/gRPC :4317--> collector pods --> CloudWatch Logs, Loki, ...

docs.title: 1. Run a collector
docs.text:
Run an OpenTelemetry Collector in the cluster with an OTLP gRPC receiver on port 4317, behind a Service. Make sure the Service has ready endpoints before you point the sink at it.

To write to CloudWatch Logs, use the collector's awscloudwatchlogs exporter, and give the collector's service account an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that can write to your log group.

docs.title: 2. Allow the proxy to reach the collector pods
docs.text:
Allow TCP 4317 into your node security group (or the collector pods' security group) from the backend security group. For example, with the EKS cluster security group:

NODE_SG=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --query 'cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.clusterSecurityGroupId' --output text)

aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $NODE_SG \
  --ip-permissions "IpProtocol=tcp,FromPort=4317,ToPort=4317,UserIdGroupPairs=[{GroupId=$BACKEND_SG,Description=elb-proxy-otlp}]"

docs.title: 3. Configure the sink
docs.text:
Point the sink at the collector Service with backendRefs. Envoy Gateway resolves it to the collector's pod IPs, which the proxy can reach directly in the VPC:

apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: EnvoyProxy
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy
  namespace: envoy-gateway-system
spec:
  telemetry:
    accessLog:
      settings:
        - type: Route
          format:
            type: Text
            text: "[%START_TIME%] \"%REQ(:METHOD)% %REQ(X-ENVOY-ORIGINAL-PATH?:PATH)% %PROTOCOL%\" %RESPONSE_CODE% %RESPONSE_FLAGS% %BYTES_RECEIVED% %BYTES_SENT% %DURATION% %RESPONSE_DURATION% \"%REQ(X-FORWARDED-FOR)%\" \"%REQ(USER-AGENT)%\" \"%REQ(X-REQUEST-ID)%\" \"%REQ(:AUTHORITY)%\" \"%UPSTREAM_HOST%\"\n"
          sinks:
            - type: OpenTelemetry
              openTelemetry:
                backendRefs:
                  - kind: Service
                    name: otel-collector
                    namespace: observability
                    port: 4317
                resources:
                  service.name: elb-proxy

Envoy Gateway sends access-log changes to the proxy over xDS. The proxy isn't replaced.

docs.title: Text or JSON
docs.text:
• format.type: Text puts the formatted line in the log record's body. To write the line to CloudWatch as-is, set raw_log: true on the awscloudwatchlogs exporter.
  • format.type: JSON puts each field in the log record's attributes and leaves the body empty. Turn raw_log off, or CloudWatch receives empty lines.
          format:
            type: JSON
            json:
              start_time: "%START_TIME%"
              method: "%REQ(:METHOD)%"
              path: "%REQ(X-ENVOY-ORIGINAL-PATH?:PATH)%"
              response_code: "%RESPONSE_CODE%"
              response_flags: "%RESPONSE_FLAGS%"
              duration: "%DURATION%"
              upstream_time: "%RESPONSE_DURATION%"
              client_ip: "%DOWNSTREAM_REMOTE_ADDRESS_WITHOUT_PORT%"
              host: "%REQ(:AUTHORITY)%"
              request_id: "%REQ(X-REQUEST-ID)%"
              upstream_host: "%UPSTREAM_HOST%"

Upstream latency

Envoy's default text format includes %RESP(X-ENVOY-UPSTREAM-SERVICE-TIME)%. The proxy removes that header, so the field is always -. Use %RESPONSE_DURATION% for upstream latency, as in the examples above.

docs.title: File sinks
docs.text:
The managed proxy doesn't support the File access logger, so a File sink, such as Envoy Gateway's default /dev/stdout, doesn't work. The controller rejects it: the Gateway gets a FailedDeployModel Warning event, and the controller creates no new proxy.

The controller can't stop Envoy Gateway from sending the listener to a proxy that already exists, though. If you switch a running proxy's EnvoyProxy to a File sink, the Gateway gets the same FailedDeployModel event. Envoy rejects the update because it has no envoy.access_loggers.file implementation, and keeps serving the last good listener. Traffic keeps working, logs keep arriving in the old format, and route changes still apply, but listener changes don't, until you fix the EnvoyProxy. The rejection only shows in Envoy Gateway's logs:

kubectl logs -n envoy-gateway-system deployment/envoy-gateway -c envoy-gateway --tail=100 \
  | grep -i rejected

Reapply a working sink to recover. No restart is needed.

docs.title: Push metrics with OpenTelemetry
docs.text: The proxy can export metrics with Envoy's OpenTelemetry stats sink. The controller writes the sink into the proxy's bootstrap. For metrics, point the sink at a stable address, such as an internal NLB in front of the collector: with backendRefs, the controller writes only the first resolved endpoint into the bootstrap, so metrics go to one collector pod.

docs.title: Install a collector
docs.text:
Envoy Gateway's add-ons Helm chart installs Prometheus, Grafana, and an OpenTelemetry Collector. Expose the collector through an internal NLB. This uses the AWS Load Balancer Controller, which must be installed in the cluster:

helm install eg-addons oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-addons-helm --version v1.10.0 \
  -n monitoring --create-namespace \
  --set opentelemetry-collector.enabled=true \
  --set opentelemetry-collector.service.type=LoadBalancer \
  --set opentelemetry-collector.service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/aws-load-balancer-type"=external \
  --set opentelemetry-collector.service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type"=ip \
  --set opentelemetry-collector.service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme"=internal \
  --set opentelemetry-collector.config.exporters.prometheus.endpoint=0.0.0.0:19001 \
  --set-string 'opentelemetry-collector.podAnnotations.prometheus\.io/scrape=true' \
  --set-string 'opentelemetry-collector.podAnnotations.prometheus\.io/port=19001'
  • aws-load-balancer-type: external hands the Service to the AWS Load Balancer Controller. It doesn't make the NLB public: aws-load-balancer-scheme does, and internal is enough because the proxy is in the same VPC. Set these annotations when you create the Service; the AWS Load Balancer Controller documents that changing aws-load-balancer-type on an existing Service can leak resources.
  • The prometheus.io annotations let the bundled Prometheus scrape the collector.

  • For a proxy with many routes, raise the collector's gRPC message limit from the 4 MB default:

    --set opentelemetry-collector.config.receivers.otlp.protocols.grpc.max_recv_msg_size_mib=16

Get the collector's NLB hostname:

kubectl get svc -n monitoring -l app.kubernetes.io/name=opentelemetry-collector \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}'

docs.title: Allow the proxy to reach the collector
docs.text: With the Service from the previous step, you don't need to add a rule. The AWS Load Balancer Controller creates a security group for the NLB that allows the Service's ports, including 4317, from 0.0.0.0/0. If you restrict the sources, for example with loadBalancerSourceRanges, or you use your own security group on the NLB, allow inbound TCP 4317 on it from the backend security group, or from your own security groups if you set them.

docs.title: Enable the sink
docs.text:
apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: EnvoyProxy
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy
  namespace: envoy-gateway-system
spec:
  telemetry:
    accessLog:
      disable: true
    metrics:
      sinks:
        - type: OpenTelemetry
          openTelemetry:
            host: <collector-nlb-hostname>
            port: 4317

Set host to an address the proxy can reach from the VPC. Cluster DNS names such as otel-collector.monitoring.svc don't resolve on the proxy.

docs.title: Grafana dashboards
docs.text:
The add-ons chart includes Envoy dashboards written for Envoy's Prometheus endpoint. Metrics sent through the OpenTelemetry sink are named differently, so the dashboards need changes:

  • There's no envoy_ prefix. For example, envoy_server_live arrives as server_live.
  • The collector's Prometheus exporter adds _total to counters that don't already end in it, for example cluster_upstream_rq_xx becomes cluster_upstream_rq_xx_total.

docs.title: Pull metrics with Prometheus
docs.text:
The proxy serves Envoy's Prometheus stats on port 19001 at /stats/prometheus. It's on by default. To turn it off, set telemetry.metrics.prometheus.disable: true in the EnvoyProxy.

Reaching the port needs your own security groups:

Managed security groups don't open 19001

The frontend security group the controller manages only allows the Gateway's listener ports, and on every reconcile it removes rules it didn't create. A rule you add manually for 19001 is removed again. To scrape the proxy, set spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups and allow 19001 from your scraper there. With your own security groups, you manage all inbound rules, including the listener ports. See Security groups.

The proxy's IP addresses can change at any time, for example as it scales. Keep your scrape targets current, for example by resolving the Gateway's address or by looking up the proxy's network interfaces with the EC2 DescribeNetworkInterfaces API.

Because of these two requirements, the OpenTelemetry sink is usually simpler.

docs.title: No access logs arrive, and nothing reports an error
docs.text:
1. Check the node security group allows TCP 4317 from the backend security group. See step 2.
  2. Check that Envoy accepted the listener: look for rejected in Envoy Gateway's logs, as in File sinks.
  3. Check that the collector receives anything at all, for example with the collector's debug exporter.

docs.title: The Gateway shows Accepted=False with InvalidParameters after adding a sink
docs.text:
The sink's backendRefs Service has no ready endpoints. Check the collector pods are running and the Service selects them:

kubectl get endpoints <collector-service> -n <collector-namespace>

docs.title: The metrics sink times out
docs.text:
If the proxy's otel_metric_sink_0 cluster shows a high upstream_cx_connect_timeout:

  1. Check that the collector NLB exists and has healthy targets:

    kubectl get svc -n monitoring -l app.kubernetes.io/name=opentelemetry-collector

  2. Check that the collector NLB's security group allows TCP 4317 from the proxy. By default it allows it from 0.0.0.0/0. If you restricted the sources, allow the backend security group.

  3. Check that host in the EnvoyProxy sink is the NLB hostname, not a cluster DNS name.

docs.title: No metrics in Prometheus
docs.text:
1. Check that the collector pod is running and has the prometheus.io/scrape annotation:

    kubectl get pods -n monitoring -l app.kubernetes.io/name=opentelemetry-collector \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.annotations}'

  2. Check that the collector's Prometheus exporter has data:

    POD_IP=$(kubectl get pod -n monitoring -l app.kubernetes.io/name=opentelemetry-collector \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.podIP}')
kubectl run check --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  curl -s http://${POD_IP}:19001/metrics | grep -c "cluster_"

docs.title: received message larger than max
docs.text:
The proxy is sending more metrics than the collector's gRPC limit allows. Raise it:

helm upgrade eg-addons oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-addons-helm --version v1.10.0 \
  -n monitoring --reuse-values \
  --set opentelemetry-collector.config.receivers.otlp.protocols.grpc.max_recv_msg_size_mib=32

docs.title: ELBProxyConfiguration
docs.text:
ELBProxyConfiguration tells the controller to run a Gateway on an AWS managed proxy, and how to configure that proxy. It's a Gateway API policy: it attaches to Gateways or GatewayClasses through spec.targetRefs.

A Gateway without an ELBProxyConfiguration has no AWS proxy.

Note

The API version is v1alpha1. Check the release notes before you upgrade.

For every field, see the Specification.

docs.title: Target a Gateway
docs.text:
Put the ELBProxyConfiguration in the same namespace as the Gateway:

apiVersion: gateway.elbproxy.aws/v1alpha1
kind: ELBProxyConfiguration
metadata:
  name: my-proxy
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      name: my-gateway
  roleArn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-proxy-role
  networkConfiguration: {}

docs.title: Target a GatewayClass
docs.text:
To apply one configuration to every Gateway in a class, target the GatewayClass. The ELBProxyConfiguration must live in the Envoy Gateway namespace (by default envoy-gateway-system):

apiVersion: gateway.elbproxy.aws/v1alpha1
kind: ELBProxyConfiguration
metadata:
  name: class-default
  namespace: envoy-gateway-system
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: GatewayClass
      name: elb-proxy-aws
  roleArn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-proxy-role
  networkConfiguration: {}

Each Gateway in the class still has its own proxy, unless you use merged gateways.

If a GatewayClass-scoped ELBProxyConfiguration is in any other namespace, it's ignored and its status shows Accepted=False with reason InvalidTargetRef.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
When several ELBProxyConfigurations match one Gateway:

  1. A Gateway-scoped one takes precedence over a GatewayClass-scoped one.
  2. Within the same scope, the oldest takes precedence (by creation time, then namespace, then name).

The others show Accepted=False with reason Conflicted.

docs.title: Merged gateways
docs.text:
With Envoy Gateway's merged gateways mode, all Gateways in a class share one proxy, and so one address. Only GatewayClass-scoped ELBProxyConfigurations apply in this mode. Gateway-scoped ones are ignored.

To use it, set mergeGateways: true on the EnvoyProxy that the GatewayClass references, and target the GatewayClass from an ELBProxyConfiguration in the Envoy Gateway namespace. The controller then creates one proxy for the class, with one frontend security group that allows the listener ports of all the Gateways. Events for the proxy appear on every Gateway in the class.

For a complete walkthrough with two Gateways on one proxy, see Merged Gateways.

docs.title: Addressability
docs.text:
spec.networkConfiguration.ipConfiguration.ipAddressingConfiguration sets whether the proxy is reachable from the internet or only inside the virtual private cloud (VPC). Each of ipv4Addressability and ipv6Addressability can be off, internal, or internet-facing.

If you don't set them, the defaults come from the spec.ipFamily field of the EnvoyProxy. The following table shows the defaults.

ipFamily IPv4 IPv6 IPv4 (default) internal off IPv6 off internal DualStack internal internal

Warning

  • The IP configuration can't be changed on an existing proxy. If you change it, the controller replaces the proxy. The same happens if you change the ipFamily field of the EnvoyProxy while you haven't set ipv4Addressability and ipv6Addressability explicitly. The controller deletes the old proxy and creates a new one with a new address. See Change subnets on an existing proxy.
  • Quote "off" in YAML. Unquoted, it's read as the boolean false.
  • The API rejects these combinations: both off, IPv4 internet-facing with IPv6 internal, and IPv4 internal with IPv6 internet-facing.

docs.title: Subnets
docs.text:
If you don't set spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.subnets, the controller discovers subnets in the cluster's VPC with the kubernetes.io/role/elb (internet-facing) or kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb (internal) tag, one for each Availability Zone, at least two. An existing proxy keeps its subnets. See Subnet discovery for the full rules, and how to tag subnets.

To choose subnets yourself, list at least two, in different Availability Zones, in the same VPC:

spec:
  networkConfiguration:
    vpcConfiguration:
      subnets:
        - subnetId: subnet-0123456789abcdef0
        - subnetId: subnet-0fedcba9876543210

When IPv6 is enabled, the subnets need IPv6 CIDR blocks.

docs.title: Security groups
docs.text:
By default, the controller creates and manages a frontend security group for the proxy. It allows inbound traffic on each listener port from:

  • spec.ingressCidrs: IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs. Defaults to 0.0.0.0/0, plus ::/0 when the proxy has IPv6 enabled.
  • spec.ingressPrefixLists: AWS prefix list IDs.
spec:
  ingressCidrs:
    - 10.0.0.0/8
  ingressPrefixLists:
    - pl-0123456789abcdef0

The controller removes inbound rules it didn't create, so don't add rules to this security group manually.

To use your own security groups, set spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups. The controller then doesn't manage any security group rules. See Security groups for both modes, what you need to allow, and switching between them.

docs.title: Other settings
docs.text:
The following table describes the other settings you can set.

Field Description roleArn Required. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role the proxy uses when Envoy filters or extensions call AWS services. Changing it replaces the proxy, which changes the Gateway's address. name Proxy name, up to 32 characters. Generated if unset. Changing it creates a new proxy and deletes the old one, which changes the Gateway's address. attributes Proxy attributes as key-value pairs. See Attributes. tags AWS tags on the proxy. These take precedence over --default-tags. Don't use keys that start with gateway.elbproxy.aws/. customerKmsKeyArn Customer managed KMS key used to encrypt the proxy's configuration. Defaults to a key that the service owns. See Customer managed KMS keys.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
The controller passes each entry in spec.attributes to ELB for Envoy without checking the key, so any attribute the service supports works. For the full list, see the ELB for Envoy API reference. The following table lists attributes that this page covers.

Key Description deletion_protection.enabled When true, the proxy can't be deleted. Default false. waf.web_acl_arn ARN of your own AWS WAF web ACL to protect the proxy. Set it when the proxy is created. To change or remove it later, use the AWS WAF API. See AWS WAF. waf.fail_open.enabled When true, the proxy lets requests through if WAF is unavailable. Default false. 
spec:
  attributes:
    - key: waf.web_acl_arn
      value: arn:aws:wafv2:us-west-2:111122223333:regional/webacl/my-acl/a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-EXAMPLE11111

How the controller applies attributes:

  • It updates a changed attribute on the existing proxy.
  • If you remove an attribute from the spec, the controller resets it to its default value, when it has one.
  • An attribute that can't be changed after creation, such as waf.web_acl_arn, fails with an error if you change it. The error appears as a FailedDeployModel event on the Gateway.
  • The controller sets the Envoy log level from EnvoyProxy.spec.logging.level, so it rejects envoy.log_level and envoy.component_log_level here.

docs.title: EnvoyProxy requirements
docs.text:
The controller reads the EnvoyProxy that Envoy Gateway uses for the Gateway. Disable access logging, or send it to a network sink such as OpenTelemetry or the Access Log Service (ALS):

apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: EnvoyProxy
spec:
  telemetry:
    accessLog:
      disable: true

The controller rejects a file sink, including Envoy Gateway's default /dev/stdout, because the path doesn't exist on the managed proxy.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
The ELBProxyConfiguration has two conditions.

Accepted says whether it applies to any Gateway. The following table lists its statuses and reasons.

Status Reason Meaning True Accepted Applied to at least one Gateway. False Conflicted Another ELBProxyConfiguration wins for the same target. False InvalidTargetRef Targets a GatewayClass but isn't in the Envoy Gateway namespace.

Programmed summarizes the AWS proxies behind it. It's True when at least one of them is active, with a message such as 2 of 3 backing proxies are active. When it targets several Gateways, check each one in status.proxies.

docs.title: Per-proxy status
docs.text:
status.proxies has one entry per target Gateway. A merged GatewayClass has a single entry with kind: GatewayClass. Each entry has the proxy's Amazon Resource Name (ARN) and its own Programmed condition:

status:
  proxies:
    - gatewayRef:
        kind: Gateway
        namespace: default
        name: my-gateway
      proxyArn: arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:us-west-2:111122223333:proxy/elbp-...
      conditions:
        - type: Programmed
          status: "False"
          reason: Pending
          message: Proxy is being created

The following table lists the possible values of the per-proxy Programmed condition.

Status Reason Meaning True Programmed The proxy is active. False Pending The proxy is being created. False ActionRequired The proxy needs action. The message lists the reasons from AWS, in the form <code>: <message> [<target>]. False CreateFailed The proxy failed to create. False Deleting The proxy is being deleted, because the Gateway was deleted, or because it is being replaced and the new proxy has the same name (you set spec.name).

While the controller updates a proxy, its entry keeps its last condition. When you delete the Gateway, the controller removes its entry once the proxy is gone. When a proxy is replaced under the same name, the entry shows Deleting until the old proxy is gone, then Pending for the new proxy. When the replacement has a different name, the controller creates the new proxy right away. An ELBProxyConfiguration reports at most 32 proxies; past that, the controller logs status.proxies is full and doesn't add more entries.

kubectl get elbproxyconfiguration <name> -n <namespace> \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.proxies[*]}{.gatewayRef.namespace}/{.gatewayRef.name}{"  "}{.conditions[?(@.type=="Programmed")].reason}{": "}{.conditions[?(@.type=="Programmed")].message}{"\n"}{end}'

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
The controller also writes events on the Gateway. The following table lists them.

Reason Type Meaning SuccessfullyReconciled Normal The controller applied the configuration to AWS. It doesn't mean the proxy is active; check per-proxy status. FailedDeployModel Warning The controller couldn't create or update the proxy. The message has the error. WaitingForProxyDeletion Normal A previous proxy is still being deleted. The new one is created after it's gone. 
kubectl describe gateway <name> -n <namespace>

docs.title: ELBProxyConfiguration
docs.text:
ELBProxyConfiguration is a CRD for ELB for Envoy proxy configuration.

ELBProxyConfiguration is a direct Gateway API policy: it attaches to one or more Gateway or GatewayClass resources via spec.targetRefs. When a Gateway is targeted, the ELBProxyConfiguration must live in the same namespace as the Gateway.

When a GatewayClass is targeted, the ELBProxyConfiguration must live in the controller's own namespace GatewayClass-scope targetRefs from ELBProxyConfigurations in any other namespace are ignored.

Field Description Default Validation apiVersion string gateway.elbproxy.aws/v1alpha1 kind string ELBProxyConfiguration metadata ObjectMeta Refer to Kubernetes API documentation for fields of metadata. spec ELBProxyConfigurationSpec status ELBProxyConfigurationStatus

docs.title: ProxyStatusEntry
docs.text:
ProxyStatusEntry reports the health of one AWS proxy backing this ELBProxyConfiguration for a specific target Gateway.

After Deleting, the entry is removed on Gateway deletion, or moves to Pending on replacement.

docs.title: TLS certificates
docs.text:
The proxy terminates TLS at its Envoy listener. Certificates follow the standard Gateway API model: you store each one in a kubernetes.io/tls Secret and reference it from the Gateway listener. Envoy Gateway sends the certificate to the proxy over xDS, so a rotated Secret reaches the proxy without replacing it.

This page covers three ways to get a certificate into that Secret:

  • cert-manager with Let's Encrypt: free certificates, issued and renewed through ACME.
  • ACM exportable certificates: certificates from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), exported into a Secret by AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK).
  • Your own certificate: a certificate and key you already have.

All three end with the same listener configuration, shown in Bind the certificate to a Gateway.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Follow Getting Started first. The examples here use its elb-proxy-aws GatewayClass.
  • The controller-managed security group opens each listener port to spec.ingressCidrs (default 0.0.0.0/0, plus ::/0 with IPv6). An HTTPS listener on port 443 is opened automatically. See Security groups.

  • Point your domain's DNS at the Gateway's address, which is the proxy's DNS name, for example, with a CNAME record:

    kubectl get gateway <name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[0].value}'

docs.title: cert-manager with Let's Encrypt
docs.text: The cert-manager project issues and renews certificates in the cluster. With Let's Encrypt, the certificates are free and trusted by browsers.

docs.title: Install cert-manager
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.17.2/cert-manager.yaml
kubectl rollout status deployment cert-manager -n cert-manager --timeout=120s
kubectl rollout status deployment cert-manager-webhook -n cert-manager --timeout=120s

Enable cert-manager's Gateway API support. The HTTP-01 challenge below needs it:

kubectl patch deployment cert-manager -n cert-manager --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--enable-gateway-api"}
]'
kubectl rollout status deployment cert-manager -n cert-manager --timeout=120s

docs.title: Create a ClusterIssuer
docs.text:
This issuer answers HTTP-01 challenges through your Gateway:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: you@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account
    solvers:
      - http01:
          gatewayHTTPRoute:
            parentRefs:
              - name: <gateway-name>
                namespace: <gateway-namespace>
                kind: Gateway

HTTP-01 requirements

Let's Encrypt connects to http://<your-domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/... from the internet. For that to reach the proxy:

  • The proxy must be internet-facing. The default is internal, so set ipv4Addressability: internet-facing in the ELBProxyConfiguration. See Addressability.
  • The Gateway needs an HTTP listener on port 80, and spec.ingressCidrs must allow the internet on it.
  • Your domain's DNS must already point at the Gateway's address.

For internal proxies or wildcard certificates, use a DNS-01 solver instead. See the cert-manager ACME documentation.

docs.title: Request a certificate
docs.text:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: gateway-tls
  namespace: <gateway-namespace>
spec:
  secretName: gateway-tls
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  dnsNames:
    - your-domain.example.com

After the challenge completes, cert-manager writes the certificate to the gateway-tls Secret. Check progress with:

kubectl get certificate gateway-tls -n <gateway-namespace>

READY turns True once the certificate is issued. Then bind it to the Gateway with certificateRefs name gateway-tls.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text: Before the certificate expires, cert-manager renews it and updates the Secret in place. Envoy Gateway sends the new certificate to the proxy. Nothing else is needed. See cert-manager certificate renewal.

docs.title: ACM exportable certificates
docs.text: AWS Certificate Manager can issue public certificates that can be exported. The ACK ACM controller requests the certificate and exports it, with its private key, into a Kubernetes Secret. It also keeps the Secret up to date when ACM renews the certificate. For the full walkthrough, see Secure Kubernetes workloads with ACM certificates in the ACM User Guide.

docs.title: Enable ACK as an EKS capability
docs.text:
Create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for the ACK capability:

cat > ack-trust-policy.json << 'EOF'
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"Service": "capabilities.eks.amazonaws.com"},
      "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"]
    }
  ]
}
EOF

aws iam create-role \
  --role-name ACKCapabilityRole \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://ack-trust-policy.json

cat > ack-acm-policy.json << EOF
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "RequestCertificates",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "acm:RequestCertificate",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ManageCertificates",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "acm:DescribeCertificate",
        "acm:UpdateCertificateOptions",
        "acm:DeleteCertificate",
        "acm:ExportCertificate",
        "acm:AddTagsToCertificate",
        "acm:RemoveTagsFromCertificate",
        "acm:ListTagsForCertificate"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:acm:$AWS_REGION:$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:certificate/*"
    }
  ]
}
EOF
aws iam put-role-policy \
  --role-name ACKCapabilityRole \
  --policy-name ACKCertificateManager \
  --policy-document file://ack-acm-policy.json
This policy lets the ACK controller request public certificates, and manage and export the certificates in your account and Region. It is based on the recommended policy of the ACK ACM controller, without the permissions for imported certificates, private certificates, and ACME endpoints. If the controller reports AccessDenied for another ACM action, add that action to the policy.

Create the capability and wait for it to become ACTIVE:

aws eks create-capability \
  --region $AWS_REGION \
  --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --capability-name ack \
  --type ACK \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:role/ACKCapabilityRole \
  --delete-propagation-policy RETAIN

aws eks describe-capability \
  --region $AWS_REGION \
  --cluster-name $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --capability-name ack \
  --query 'capability.status' --output text

Check that the ACM resource types are available:

kubectl api-resources | grep acm.services.k8s.aws

docs.title: Request and export the certificate
docs.text:
Create an empty kubernetes.io/tls Secret for the export, and a Certificate that exports into it:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
type: kubernetes.io/tls
metadata:
  name: acm-gateway-tls
  namespace: <gateway-namespace>
data:
  tls.crt: ""
  tls.key: ""
---
apiVersion: acm.services.k8s.aws/v1alpha1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: gateway-cert
  namespace: <gateway-namespace>
spec:
  domainName: your-domain.example.com
  options:
    certificateTransparencyLoggingPreference: ENABLED
  exportTo:
    namespace: <gateway-namespace>
    name: acm-gateway-tls
    key: tls.crt

ACM issues a public certificate only after you validate the domain, by DNS or email. See ACM domain validation. Once it's issued, the ACK controller writes the certificate and private key to acm-gateway-tls. Then bind it to the Gateway with certificateRefs name acm-gateway-tls.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text: ACM renews eligible certificates before they expire. With exportTo set, the ACK controller updates the Secret with the renewed certificate, and Envoy Gateway sends it to the proxy. Nothing else is needed.

docs.title: Your own certificate
docs.text:
If you already have a certificate and private key, such as one from your own certificate authority, create the Secret yourself. Put the full chain in the certificate file:

kubectl create secret tls gateway-tls -n <gateway-namespace> \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key

Then bind it to the Gateway with certificateRefs name gateway-tls.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
To rotate the certificate, update the Secret with the new files:

kubectl create secret tls gateway-tls -n <gateway-namespace> \
  --cert=new-tls.crt --key=new-tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

Envoy Gateway sends the new certificate to the proxy, which serves it within seconds. The proxy isn't replaced.

docs.title: Bind the certificate to a Gateway
docs.text:
Reference the Secret from an HTTPS listener:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: my-gateway
  namespace: <gateway-namespace>
spec:
  gatewayClassName: elb-proxy-aws
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - kind: Secret
            name: gateway-tls  # or acm-gateway-tls

The proxy serves routes attached to this listener with the certificate. The same certificateRefs work on a TLS listener with mode: Terminate for TLSRoute. For mode: Passthrough, the proxy forwards TLS to the backend unchanged and needs no certificate.

Check that the Gateway accepted the certificate. ResolvedRefs is False in three cases: the Secret is missing, it isn't of type kubernetes.io/tls, or it's in another namespace without a ReferenceGrant:

kubectl get gateway my-gateway -n <gateway-namespace> \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.listeners[*]}{.name}{": "}{range .conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {end}{"\n"}{end}'

Then test the connection:

curl -v https://your-domain.example.com/

Secret in another namespace

To use a Secret from a different namespace, add namespace to the certificateRefs entry. Then create a Gateway API ReferenceGrant in the Secret's namespace that allows Gateways from the Gateway's namespace to reference Secrets.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
This page helps you diagnose common problems with the sidecar, the controller, and ELBProxyConfiguration resources. Start with the quick checks, then find your symptom in the following sections.

Prerequisites: install the controller and deploy the example

  1. Install the controller and Envoy Gateway by following the Installation Guide.

  2. Deploy the example Gateway from Getting Started, or set it up in one go:

    export PROXY_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-proxy-role

cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: EnvoyProxy
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy
  namespace: envoy-gateway-system
spec:
  ipFamily: IPv4
  telemetry:
    accessLog:
      disable: true
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: elb-proxy-aws
spec:
  controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/gatewayclass-controller
  parametersRef:
    group: gateway.envoyproxy.io
    kind: EnvoyProxy
    name: elb-proxy
    namespace: envoy-gateway-system
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: echo
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: echo
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: echo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: echo
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: echo
          image: registry.k8s.io/gateway-api/echo-basic:v1.5.1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: echo
spec:
  selector:
    app: echo
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: echo-gateway
  namespace: echo
spec:
  gatewayClassName: elb-proxy-aws
  listeners:
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: echo
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: echo-gateway
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: echo
          port: 8080
---
apiVersion: gateway.elbproxy.aws/v1alpha1
kind: ELBProxyConfiguration
metadata:
  name: echo-proxy
  namespace: echo
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      name: echo-gateway
  roleArn: ${PROXY_ROLE_ARN}
  networkConfiguration:
    ipConfiguration:
      ipAddressingConfiguration:
        ipv4Addressability: internet-facing
        ipv6Addressability: "off"
EOF

  3. Wait for the Gateway, then save its address:

    kubectl wait gateway/echo-gateway -n echo --for=condition=Programmed --timeout=15m
export GATEWAY_HOST=$(kubectl get gateway echo-gateway -n echo \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[0].value}')
curl -i http://$GATEWAY_HOST/

docs.title: Quick checks
docs.text:
1. Is the sidecar running in the Envoy Gateway pod?

kubectl get pods -n envoy-gateway-system \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{": "}{.spec.initContainers[*].name}{"\n"}{end}'

Each Envoy Gateway pod should list elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider.

2. What does the sidecar log say?

kubectl logs -n envoy-gateway-system deployment/envoy-gateway \
  -c elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider --tail=200

Only one sidecar, the leader, calls AWS. If you run several Envoy Gateway replicas, check each pod, or find the leader:

kubectl get lease elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-leader \
  -n envoy-gateway-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.holderIdentity}{"\n"}'

3. Is the ELBProxyConfiguration accepted, and are its proxies active?

kubectl get elbproxyconfiguration -A \
  -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,ACCEPTED:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Accepted")].reason,PROGRAMMED:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Programmed")].message'

PROGRAMMED shows a message such as 1 of 2 backing proxies are active. If any proxy isn't active, check its entry in status.proxies. See Check the proxy's status.

4. What do the Gateway events say?

kubectl describe gateway <name> -n <namespace>

Look for SuccessfullyReconciled, FailedDeployModel, or WaitingForProxyDeletion events from elbproxy-gateway-extension.

docs.title: Envoy Gateway pods don't have the sidecar
docs.text:
Envoy Gateway Helm values (default)Webhook
  • Check that Envoy Gateway was installed or upgraded with your filled-in eg-values.yaml (helm get values eg -n envoy-gateway-system), and that it includes the deployment.pod.initContainers sidecar.
  • Check that you're on Envoy Gateway v1.10 or later. Older charts ignore deployment.pod.initContainers.

The webhook only adds the sidecar when a pod is created.

  • If you installed the chart after Envoy Gateway, restart Envoy Gateway:

    kubectl rollout restart deployment envoy-gateway -n envoy-gateway-system

  • Check that envoyGatewayNamespace matches the namespace Envoy Gateway runs in. The webhook ignores pods in other namespaces.

  • Check that webhook.enabled=true is set and the webhook is running:

    kubectl get deployment -n elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider-system

docs.title: Envoy Gateway pods can't be created
docs.text:
Events on the Envoy Gateway ReplicaSet show failed calling webhook "mpod.gateway.elbproxy.aws".

With the default webhook.failurePolicy: Fail, Envoy Gateway pods can't be created while the webhook is unavailable. Fix the webhook deployment first. The ReplicaSet retries on its own once it's back.

docs.title: The sidecar keeps restarting
docs.text:
Check the sidecar's previous logs:

kubectl logs -n envoy-gateway-system <envoy-gateway-pod> \
  -c elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider --previous

The following table lists common startup errors and their fixes.

Error Fix region not resolved; specify --aws-region or set AWS_REGION / AWS_DEFAULT_REGION Set the sidecar's --aws-region: in eg-values.yaml (default), or aws.region in the chart values (webhook). NODENAME "..." is not an instance ID; set --aws-vpc-id or --aws-vpc-tags Set the sidecar's --aws-vpc-id: in eg-values.yaml (default), or aws.vpcId in the chart values (webhook). resolved VPC ID is empty, no VPC found with tags, or multiple VPCs found with tags Set --aws-vpc-id, or make the VPC tags match exactly one VPC. --sidecar-image is required when --enable-sidecar-webhook is set The webhook deployment has no sidecar image. The chart sets it from image.repository and image.tag, so check those values. tag key "..." cannot be specified in --default-tags (reserved by controller) A reserved gateway.elbproxy.aws/ key is in --default-tags or --external-managed-tags, or a key is in both flags. Remove it. See Configurations. AccessDenied or UnauthorizedOperation Envoy Gateway's service account doesn't have the controller AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy. See Installation Guide Step 2. With IRSA, check the annotation is still on the service account: helm uninstall eg removes it. After fixing, restart Envoy Gateway so the pod gets credentials.

docs.title: The Gateway has no address
docs.text:
Work through these in order.

No ELBProxyConfiguration attached. The controller only creates a proxy for a Gateway that has an ELBProxyConfiguration. The sidecar logs ELBProxyConfiguration not resolved, skipping reconcile. Check that:

  • spec.targetRefs names the Gateway exactly, with group: gateway.networking.k8s.io and kind: Gateway.
  • The ELBProxyConfiguration is in the same namespace as the Gateway.
  • For a GatewayClass target, the ELBProxyConfiguration is in the Envoy Gateway namespace.

The ELBProxyConfiguration isn't accepted. See Accepted is False.

The deploy failed before a proxy was created. Look for a FailedDeployModel event on the Gateway. See FailedDeployModel errors.

The proxy exists but isn't active. Check its status. See Check the proxy's status. Envoy Gateway shows this on the Gateway as Programmed=False with reason AddressNotAssigned.

docs.title: Check the proxy's status
docs.text:
Once a proxy exists, its state is in the ELBProxyConfiguration's status.proxies, one entry per Gateway, with the proxy Amazon Resource Name (ARN):

kubectl get elbproxyconfiguration <name> -n <namespace> \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.proxies[*]}{.gatewayRef.namespace}/{.gatewayRef.name}{"  "}{.proxyArn}{"\n    "}{.conditions[?(@.type=="Programmed")].reason}{": "}{.conditions[?(@.type=="Programmed")].message}{"\n"}{end}'

The following table lists each reason and what to do about it.

Reason What to do Programmed The proxy is active. If requests still fail, see The proxy is up but requests fail. Pending The proxy is being created, which takes several minutes. The controller checks again every 2 minutes, and the Gateway gets its address when creation finishes. If it stays Pending much longer than usual, open a support case with the proxy ARN. ActionRequired The proxy needs action from you. The message lists each reason from AWS as <code>: <message> [<target>]. Fix what it names, such as a resource in [<target>]. The condition updates on the next reconcile. CreateFailed The proxy failed to create. Check the sidecar logs around the time it was created, then open a support case with the proxy ARN. Deleting The proxy is being deleted. Proxy is being deleted means the Gateway was deleted. Replacing the proxy: deleting the old proxy means a change requires a new proxy and the new proxy has the same name (you set spec.name). The controller creates the new one after the old one is gone, and the Gateway shows WaitingForProxyDeletion meanwhile. Without spec.name, the new proxy has a new name, so the controller creates it right away.

SuccessfullyReconciled doesn't mean the proxy is healthy

With ActionRequired or CreateFailed, the controller's own work still succeeded, so the Gateway gets a SuccessfullyReconciled event, not a warning. The ELBProxyConfiguration status is the only place these states appear.

The top-level Programmed condition is True as long as any proxy is active, so with several Gateways, check each entry.

docs.title: FailedDeployModel errors
docs.text:
The event message is Failed deploy model due to followed by the error from the failing step. Errors returned by AWS appear in it too, for example failed to create proxy: .... The following table lists common ones.

Message contains Cause and fix access logging on AWS-managed proxy must either be disabled ... The Gateway's EnvoyProxy uses Envoy Gateway's default file access log. Set telemetry.accessLog.disable: true, or use an OpenTelemetry or Access Log Service (ALS) sink. unable to resolve at least one subnet No eligible subnets found. If you rely on discovery, tag at least two subnets in different Availability Zones with kubernetes.io/role/elb=1 (internet-facing) or kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1 (internal), or list subnets in spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.subnets. The message also says how many subnets were skipped for other clusters' tags, fewer than 8 free IP addresses, or (for IPv6 proxies) no IPv6 CIDR block. See Subnet discovery. subnets count less than minimal required count The proxy needs at least two subnets. multiple subnets in same Availability Zone Pick one subnet per Availability Zone. do not have an associated IPv6 CIDR block IPv6 is enabled, so every subnet needs an IPv6 CIDR. attribute "..." is read-only and cannot be changed from "..." to "..." You changed an attribute that can't change after the proxy is created. Set the original value again. For waf.web_acl_arn, change the web ACL with the AWS WAF API, then set the spec to match. See AWS WAF. attribute "..." is managed by the controller Remove the Envoy log-level attributes from spec.attributes. Set EnvoyProxy.spec.logging.level instead. tag key "..." is externally managed That tag key is in --external-managed-tags. Remove it from spec.tags. no node security groups discovered or expected exactly one SG tagged "kubernetes.io/cluster/<name>" The controller couldn't find the security groups of your nodes. Check that the nodes are Ready EC2 instances with an AWS spec.providerID. If a node's primary network interface has several security groups, tag exactly one of them kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name>. AccessDenied The controller IAM policy is missing an action, or the resource isn't tagged as controller-managed. Check the policy against k8s/iam-policy.json.

The controller retries failed deploys automatically. After you fix the cause, the next retry picks up the change.

docs.title: Accepted is False
docs.text:
The following table lists the reasons.

Reason Cause and fix Conflicted Another ELBProxyConfiguration targets the same Gateway and takes precedence. A Gateway-scoped one takes precedence over a GatewayClass-scoped one, and the oldest takes precedence within the same scope, then the lowest namespace and name. Delete or retarget one of them. InvalidTargetRef It targets a GatewayClass but isn't in the Envoy Gateway namespace. Move it to that namespace.

docs.title: Can't delete an ELBProxyConfiguration
docs.text:
The delete hangs, and the sidecar logs ELBProxyConfiguration ... is still in use by gateway ....

An ELBProxyConfiguration has a finalizer, so it can't be deleted while a Gateway uses it. Delete the Gateway first, or attach a different ELBProxyConfiguration to it.

docs.title: The proxy is up but requests fail
docs.text:
Can't connect at all.

  • An internal proxy is only reachable from inside the virtual private cloud (VPC). Use ipv4Addressability: internet-facing to reach it from outside. Changing it replaces the proxy, which gets a new address.
  • Check spec.ingressCidrs and spec.ingressPrefixLists. They limit who can reach the listener ports.
  • A new proxy's DNS name can take a few minutes to resolve.

Connects, but gets errors or no response. The proxy might not be getting its configuration, or might not reach your pods.

  • Custom security groups: if you set spec.networkConfiguration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups, the controller doesn't add any rules. See Bring your own security groups for the full list. You must allow inbound traffic from the proxy to the following:
    • Envoy Gateway pods on TCP 18000 (xDS), and on TCP 18002 (Wasm modules) if you use Wasm extensions
    • your backend pods, and any request mirror, ext_authz, or ext_proc services, on their target ports
  • Pod networking: pod IPs must be routable in the VPC. The proxy connects to pod IPs directly.

  • Route status: check that the route is accepted and its backends resolve:

    kubectl get httproute <name> -n <namespace> -o yaml

docs.title: Global rate limiting doesn't work
docs.text:
Global rate limiting isn't supported. See Compatibility. Envoy Gateway still translates a BackendTrafficPolicy with type: Global, so the proxy gets a ratelimit_cluster pointing at envoy-ratelimit.<envoy-gateway-namespace>.svc.cluster.local. That name doesn't resolve outside the cluster, so the cluster has no healthy hosts. What happens next depends on failClosed in the EnvoyGateway config's rateLimit section:

The following table shows what happens for each failClosed value.

failClosed Symptom false (default) Requests pass, and the limit isn't enforced. Nothing reports an error. true Every request on the affected routes gets HTTP 500. Other routes keep working.

The controller doesn't report either case. To fix it, delete the BackendTrafficPolicy, or change it to type: Local. The proxy drops the ratelimit_cluster and the 500s stop, with no restart. If you don't use global rate limiting, remove the rateLimit section from the EnvoyGateway config too.

docs.title: Collect information for a bug report
docs.text:
Include:

kubectl get gateway,httproute,elbproxyconfiguration -A -o yaml > resources.yaml
kubectl describe gateway -A > gateway-events.txt
kubectl logs -n envoy-gateway-system deployment/envoy-gateway \
  -c elb-envoy-remote-infra-provider --tail=1000 > sidecar.log
kubectl logs -n envoy-gateway-system deployment/envoy-gateway \
  -c envoy-gateway --tail=1000 > envoy-gateway.log

Also include the controller and Envoy Gateway versions, and the proxy ARN from status.proxies[].proxyArn if one was created. Remove account IDs, role ARNs, and other sensitive values before sharing.
